EDCS-14200138.text_edition: \n Heraclii Dignissimo principali innocentissimo puero Tito Flavio Vibiano Iuniori pontifici duumviro filio ac collegae Titi Flavi Frontini Heraclii in parvulis annis exhibenti aequaliter voluptatum genera patris sui studiis populi sufragio et decreto ordinis Divina stirpe progenito domino nostro fortissimo principi Valentiniano victori Pio Felici ac triumphatori semper Augusto Flavius Vivius Benedictus vir perfectissimus praeses provinciae Tripolitanae numini maiestatique eius semper devotus\n
EDCS-14200138.translation: To Heraclius, the most worthy, preeminent, and most innocent boy, pontiff and duumvir, son and colleague of Titus Flavius Frontinus Heraclius, showing in his young years the same pleasures as his father, by the people's suffrage and the decree of the order. Descended from a divine line, to our lord, the most brave prince, Valentinian, victorious, pious, happy, triumphant, always Augustus. Flavius Vivius Benedictus, the most perfect man, governor of the province of Tripolitana, always devoted to his divinity and majesty.
EDCS-14200138.summary: This is a dedication to a young boy, Titus Flavius Vibianus Iunior, who held priestly and civic offices, by the governor Flavius Vivius Benedictus, honoring him and the emperor Valentinian.

EDCS-14200139.translation: Boncar Mecrasi Clodius, the doctor (Greek: Bonchar Mechrasi Klodios, physician).
EDCS-14200139.summary: A bilingual inscription (Latin and Greek) identifying an individual named Clodius as a doctor, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14200140.translation: Byrycth, daughter of Balsilechis, mother of Clodius the doctor (Greek: Byrychth, daughter of Balsialech, mother of Klodios the physician).
EDCS-14200140.summary: A bilingual inscription (Latin and Greek) identifying Byrycth as the mother of Clodius the doctor mentioned in EDCS-14200139, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14200141.text_edition: \n <T=I>(ito) Axio Quirina pro liberis Celeri Tito Axio Titi filio Quirina \n
EDCS-14200141.translation: Titus Axios Quirinus, for his children, Celer, Titus Axios, son of Titus, Quirinus.
EDCS-14200141.summary: This inscription likely refers to the dedication of a monument or tomb for children named Celer and Titus Axios, by their father Titus Axios Quirinus.

EDCS-14200142.translation: To the Divine Manes of Lucius Claudius Perpetuus Probatus, who lived 20 years.
EDCS-14200142.summary: A funerary inscription recording the short life of Lucius Claudius Perpetuus Probatus, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14200143.translation: Domitia Rogata lived for 23 years. Marcus Iulius Cethegus made this for his dearest wife.
EDCS-14200143.summary: A funerary monument erected by Marcus Iulius Cethegus for his wife Domitia Rogata, who died at age 23, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14200144.translation: To the Divine Manes of the most pious M. Iulius Mamios Severus.
EDCS-14200144.summary: A funerary dedication to M. Iulius Mamios Severus, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14200145.translation: Publius Lucretius Rogatianus, son of Publius, restored this monument, which his father had made with opus signinum, for himself and his descendants, and erected it from the foundation at a cost of 80,000 sesterces.
EDCS-14200145.summary: An epitaph detailing the restoration and erection of a family tomb by Publius Lucretius Rogatianus, including the cost of the work, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14200146.translation: Celestis, most holy one, may you be propitious.
EDCS-14200146.summary: A brief votive or dedicatory inscription to a deity named Celestis, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14200148.text_edition: \n Imperatore Caesare Marco Aurelio Antonino Augusto patre patriae et Imperatore Caesare Lucio Aurelio Vero Armeniaco Augusto Servius Cornelius Scipio Salvidienus Orfitus proconsul cum Uttedio Marcello legato suo dedicavit Caius Calpurnius Celsus curator muneris publici munerarius IIvir quinquennalis flamen perpetuus arcum pecunia sua solo publico et fundavit et marmore solido fecit\n
EDCS-14200148.translation: While Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, father of the fatherland, and Emperor Caesar Lucius Aurelius Verus Armeniacus Augustus were in office, Servius Cornelius Scipio Salvidienus Orfitus, proconsul, with his legate Uttedius Marcellus, dedicated. Caius Calpurnius Celsus, curator of the public duty, twice munerarius, duumvir for five years, perpetual priest, founded and built the arch from his own money on public land with solid marble.
EDCS-14200148.summary: This inscription records the dedication of an arch, built and funded by Caius Calpurnius Celsus, during the joint reign of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, and the proconsulship of Servius Cornelius Scipio Salvidienus Orfitus.

EDCS-14200150.translation: To the Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Pius Felix Augustus, by public decree of the Gigthenses.
EDCS-14200150.summary: This inscription is a public dedication by the people of Gigthis to Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Pius Felix Augustus, likely set up during his reign (161-180 AD).

EDCS-14200151.translation: To Quintus, perpetual flamen and priest of the province, may our lords Flavius Valentinianus, Theodosius, Arcadius, and Maximus, always Augusti, conquerors of the whole world, be safe. Quintus, a man of laudable priestly standing, wishing to respond to this with appropriate merits, on account of the magnificent legation which he executed and completed on behalf of the vows of the entire province, and by decree of our council and our order, with money allocated from public funds.
EDCS-14200151.summary: This inscription honors Quintus, a high-ranking priest and official, for his service to the province and the emperors Valentinian I, Theodosius I, Arcadius, and Honorius (late 4th/early 5th century AD).

EDCS-14200152.translation: Although the council had decreed a statue for Gaius Ummidius Sedatus, son of Marcus, of the Quirina tribe, Marcus Ummidius Sedatus, content with the honor, erected it at his own expense.
EDCS-14200152.summary: This inscription records that Marcus Ummidius Sedatus erected a statue at his own expense for his father, Gaius Ummidius Sedatus, even though the town council had already decreed it, likely in the 2nd or 3rd century AD.

EDCS-14200153.translation: Gaius Ummidius Haterianus, Lucius Ummidius Pacatus, and Marcus Ummidius Sedatus erected this at their own expense to their most indulgent father, Gaius Ummidius Sedatus.
EDCS-14200153.summary: This inscription is a dedication by three sons (Gaius Ummidius Haterianus, Lucius Ummidius Pacatus, and Marcus Ummidius Sedatus) to their father, Gaius Ummidius Sedatus, at their own expense, likely in the 2nd or 3rd century AD.

EDCS-14200154.translation: To Lucius Ummidius Pacatus, by the council and people of Gigthis, with contributions from residents and inhabitants, for his manifold [---] beneficial service.
EDCS-14200154.summary: This inscription honors Lucius Ummidius Pacatus, son of Quirina, with contributions from the council, people, and residents of Gigthis, likely for his service to the community, probably in the 2nd or 3rd century AD.

EDCS-14200155.translation: To Gaius Caecilius Claudius Aelianus, perpetual suffete and flaminius, honored for his excellent service in public office and the curial position with integrity, and for his patriotism and diligent service in Rome, which brought him the highest praise from consular witnesses of distinguished repute; the town council of Gigthi, pleased by his gratuitous services, decreed that a statue should be erected, but he himself, content with the honor of the decree, arranged for its construction at his own expense.
EDCS-14200155.summary: This is a decree from the town council of Gigthi honoring Gaius Caecilius Claudius Aelianus for his integrity in public office and his service in Rome, and recording their decision to erect a statue in his honor.

EDCS-14200156.translation: The council and people took care to erect at their own expense a statue for Servaeus Honoratus, son of Quintus, of the Quirina tribe, who had discharged all the offices of his fatherland, for whom the council, at the people's request, had decreed a statue because of his munificence, and who wished to erect it himself with money remitted to the state.
EDCS-14200156.summary: This inscription records the erection of a statue for Servaeus Honoratus, commissioned by the council and people of Gigthis due to his munificence, likely in the 2nd or 3rd century AD.

EDCS-14200159.translation: To the Spirits of the Departed. M. Nimenivus (son of Masnabubas?) [erected this].
EDCS-14200159.summary: This is a fragmented funerary inscription dedicating a monument to the deceased, identified only by the names of the father and possibly the dedicator.

EDCS-14200160.translation: To the Spirits of the Departed. Lucanus, Severus, and IAM Rur, sons of Niscarcuminius, erected this for their father.
EDCS-14200160.summary: This is a funerary inscription where three sons (Lucanus, Severus, and IAM Rur) dedicate a monument to their father, Niscarcuminus.

EDCS-14200166.translation: Maius, son of [---]nicus, and his brother Fecerunt, and for themselves.
EDCS-14200166.summary: This is a funerary inscription where Maius and his brother erected a monument for themselves and possibly another individual.

EDCS-14300122.translation: Beforehand, believe that coming you are reborn by Christ's font; thus you will be able to see the kingdom of God, cleansed. He who is dipped in this sacred water will never feel death, for he who is washed by the water lives forever. Descend boldly into the fountains of perennial life; these fonts create eternal men. Ascend into heaven, soul, you who have been washed in the font; may this be perpetual for you. Extinguish your sins, burning in this font; run, why do you stand? Time and the hour flee. Calbulus, a suppliant, has presented the appearance of the offered marble and new gifts, mindful of the font from which he was reborn, and has brought the form of a deer to the embrace of the waters.
EDCS-14300122.summary: This is a metrical epigram, likely from a baptismal font or a nearby monument, praising the sacrament of baptism and mentioning Calbulus as a beneficiary who dedicated the marble. It is likely from the Christian Roman period.

EDCS-14300124.translation: King Hunerix, whose constant faith incites eternal fame, scatters a memorable deed through the ranks, which separated the waters with a single word and clove the mass of the deep by command, and naked earth is trod by swimmers; man fears to have dug the sea with hoes, the wave of the sea withdraws, and the liquid rain is dashed by tortuous windings, and they move the ocean with their hands, and the snail drinks the sea.
EDCS-14300124.summary: This poetic inscription likely celebrates a significant engineering feat, possibly the creation of a canal or harbor, attributed to King Hunerix.

EDCS-14300125.translation: Where now shining signs gleam with precious metals and the work glows with bright marble, the arid land lay squalid with dusty earth and the shore sand was worthless. But the king Thrasamund, who led beautiful high structures to the sky, vowed public joys to the people, continuing his prosperous ages by his divine power; water obeyed his commands, changing its taste, and the sweet spring flowed with new waters. Vulcan himself feared the sudden rise of the hot springs and himself quickly supplied the flames with his hand.
EDCS-14300125.summary: This inscription describes King Thrasamund's construction of magnificent baths at Baiae, transforming a barren area into a place of luxury and health, likely dating to the Vandalic period.

EDCS-14300126.translation: The noble construction of the baths of Baiae is admired, and the increased springs double the sun's rays. King Thrasamund made this work in a single year, giving splendid gifts to the people in season; here the flourishing vitality is renewed for the panting old men, here living pools soothe tired limbs, fires mix equally with the waters, and nearby fire has cold rains; this fire is useful and consumes no limbs, and heat is more desired through new wishes; this place leaves the sick by the cure of diseases and does not bathe the dying in glass waters.
EDCS-14300126.summary: This poetic epigram praises King Thrasamund's construction of the baths at Baiae, highlighting their therapeutic benefits for the elderly and infirm and their luxurious heating systems.

EDCS-14300127.translation: A royal decree erected splendid structures; lime, stone, water, and fire sensed the power. Here Vulcan is immersed in cold waters, and fire has peace with the liquid springs; the flame exists in harmony with the cold waters, and the cold nymph is amazed by the burning lakes. Here the guest is always heated and not harmed, and the doctor invigorates the chest soaked in vapor; but whoever suffers from the disgust of the sun or is heavy with moist body in the water, let him hasten to immerse himself in these Thrasamundian baths, and either affliction will immediately escape.
EDCS-14300127.summary: This inscription celebrates the therapeutic baths of Thrasamund at Baiae, emphasizing the harmonious combination of heat and water to cure ailments and refresh visitors.

EDCS-14300128.translation: He who leads public walls from high roofs, King Thrasamund, dedicated pious vows to the people, through whom all beautiful things rise from their ruins, and new heights surpass old seats. Here also, after the sacred temple and magnificent halls which he erected with sacred love, he founded immense baths under his own name; here good fire competes with abundant springs, and no one fears the face of the blazing furnace; here abundant water provides cold streams, here the heat is mild, here colds do not frighten; here the doubled day shines through white marble.
EDCS-14300128.summary: This inscription dedicates the construction of grand baths to the people by King Thrasamund, detailing the impressive architecture and the harmonious blend of heat and water, likely in Baiae.

EDCS-14300129.translation: Flow gently, nymphs, from the source of the tranquil river; here, good divinities, succeed the blazing Phoebus, where from high rocks the structures now rise, and the lofty baths are made level with the whole seats of the sky. Here the marble burns with great signs, the high and lofty baths surpass the heights; and the exceptional author of such a threshold gives these gifts, foreseeing the rewards of eternal fame. Here the flame does not harm, know the vow of the poem, learn also how much water lives beneath the whirlpool; here the Vandal name is renewed from a dear seed, under whose title grace stands for deeds done.
EDCS-14300129.summary: This poetic inscription praises the magnificent baths, possibly at Baiae, highlighting their grandeur and therapeutic qualities, and connects their renewal to the Vandal king, possibly Thrasamund.

EDCS-14300130.translation: A great hand made a large Baiae in a small space, it extended the peaks suspended by white columns, it curved the shells into chambers of various designs; the marbles shine, beautiful with solid construction, the inlay of the craftsman imitates united splendor. With a hoarse murmur, the heat seethes in the furnaces; fire dominates in the flames. The pleasant fire is safe, the bather is protected, surrounded by much fire. Miraculously, amidst harmless flames, it is possible to overcome the heat of the sun with fires. From here they seek streams flowing from an icy spring, from here heat, from there snows restore health through the limbs. Nymphs run about, rivers fill the pools; the water is rippled by the overflowing lips of glass. These are monuments for you and will remain for your descendants; and the grandfather adorned his descendants for ages; may you, however, enjoy being exalted through long times.
EDCS-14300130.summary: This inscription describes the intricate construction and beneficial effects of baths at Baiae, emphasizing the advanced engineering and the harmonious interplay of heat and water, possibly commissioned by a grandfather for his descendants.

EDCS-14300132.translation: The wondrous deed of King Hilderic shines with art, work, genius, wealth, and price; here the sun itself captures rays which it can give here; it is believed to be another day made of marble. Here the sun is without clouds, snow mixed and scattered is thought to be the ground, so that you would believe it possible to drown your feet.
EDCS-14300132.summary: This inscription praises the magnificent artistic and architectural achievements of King Hilderic, possibly referring to the baths at Baiae, which are so splendid they seem to rival the sun and create an illusion of snow.

EDCS-14300133.translation: Powerful Vandalric, heir of the twin diadems, you have adorned your name through immense deeds. The avenger Theodosius subdued warring armies, returning captive peoples with an easy victory. Honorius subjected his enemies with gentle arms, whose quickness made him better and most powerful; the renowned valor of Valentinian is shown to the world through the skill of his grandson, having subjected enemies.
EDCS-14300133.summary: This inscription honors Vandalic rulers, mentioning Theodosius and Honorius for their military victories, and praising Valentinian's grandson for continuing this legacy of power and conquest.

EDCS-14300134.translation: With health-giving fire, the boy of Venus, flaming all things, skillfully provides waters for torches.
EDCS-14300134.summary: This brief, enigmatic inscription appears to be a poetic couplet, possibly related to a religious or celebratory context, perhaps linking the god of fire (Vulcan) and love (Venus) to the provision of water or light.

EDCS-14300135.translation: How much better is your lot with your trident, Neptune, than this one; after the sea, sweet waters are given to you here.
EDCS-14300135.summary: This is a poetic epitaph that contrasts the dangers of the sea with the sweetness of fresh water, likely near a spring or fountain.

EDCS-14300136.translation: Overly cautious, the rustic woman removes the thorn from her foot with her eyes, marking the deep wound with certain lights; Cupid consoles her with the voice of a piper, mocking that she is without a male witness. Do not believe that art has played false with its figures; living bodies usually render less the appearance of reality.
EDCS-14300136.summary: This is a complex, allegorical poem inscribed on a monument, likely a tomb, discussing art, beauty, and the perception of reality, possibly related to a female subject.

EDCS-14300137.translation: Learn the pious deed: after striking down his brother Romulus, Rome is given to you; let no one now blame you by name for the slaughter of walls if the omen is fitting.
EDCS-14300137.summary: This inscription refers to the legendary founding of Rome by Romulus and Remus, commenting on the fratricide and the city's destiny.

EDCS-14300138.translation: Amidst constructed moles and high walls, a pleasant garden is present, and more fitting for its owner; here various leaves grow with vital seed, in which is health presided over by the Genius. Nothing of Phoebus or Asclepius is held by learning that must be prepared; here all care for diseases is pleasing. I think now, what place of the sky is it where the divinities reign, when these herbs are permitted to overcome the burden of death?
EDCS-14300138.summary: This is a programmatic poem describing an idyllic garden with medicinal herbs, celebrating its healing properties and its connection to divine powers, likely found in a garden or associated with a physician.

EDCS-14300140.translation: Who would not believe that rivers give these Syrtes, who gave unknown waters to drink from the mountains?
EDCS-14300140.summary: This is a short, epigrammatic verse likely inscribed on a monument, possibly a fountain or aqueduct, praising the power that brings water to arid regions.

EDCS-14300141.translation: Alas, grief, and always death, envious of great destinies, which plunges tender limbs under an unfriendly star. Damira, a royal infant, is enclosed here in a tomb, whose innocent life was cut short in her fourth year. How easily sad things obscure a pleasant light; no one will have had white roses unless she picked the good ones. She bore her young age with all praise, pleasing too much with her appearance, with a modest face, she surpassed her years with nature's wit. Whatever she spoke beforehand from her mouth, she spoke sweetly, and her tongue poured forth a murmur different from honey, just as the song of birds is accustomed to flourish in the springtime. The royal heaven possesses this pure soul, and sees her among the just companies. But while the father Oageis protects Libya with arms, he suddenly heard that his daughter had died. This news was more grievous to him than all enemies, and Victory herself wept over such a misfortune.
EDCS-14300141.summary: This is an elaborate epitaph for Damira, a royal infant who died in her fourth year, detailing her beauty, wit, and innocence, and lamenting her loss, with her father being King Oageis.

EDCS-14300143.translation: Whoever burdens the sad marble of Hilarinus with tears, let him rather weep for his hard-lived grandmother. He deserved to be chosen by the tender god, to live a brief youth, but now he is under the soldier of Christ.
EDCS-14300143.summary: This is an epitaph for Hilarinus, a young boy who died and is now considered a soldier of Christ, contrasting his short life with his grandmother's longevity and his eternal reward.

EDCS-14400004.translation: Here lies the most pleasing virgin Urbica, extinguished to her father, whose name always shines to the stars; you are snatched away from these eternal darknesses, to enjoy everlasting praise in the highest places, when an eternal day is granted to you.
EDCS-14400004.summary: This is an epitaph for Urbica, a virgin praised for her virtue and beauty, who has ascended to eternal life.

EDCS-14400007.text_edition: \n Hic posuit cineres genetrix castissima prolis Augustine tui altera lux meriti qui servans pacis caelestia iura sacerdos commissos populos moribus instituis gloria vos maior gestorum laude coronat virtutum mater felicior suboles\n
EDCS-14400007.translation: Here lies the ashes of Augustine, your most chaste mother, the other light of your merit; who, as a priest observing the heavenly laws of peace, instructed the entrusted peoples in morals; your glory, greater than the rewards of deeds, crowns you, happier mother, with the praise of virtues, you, the more fruitful offspring.
EDCS-14400007.summary: This is a funerary epigram, likely from an epitaph, praising a deceased mother, Augustine, and her son, a priest, highlighting their virtues and spiritual roles.

EDCS-14400008.translation: The body of one killed by the cruel slaughter of the Donatists is buried here. Nabor, with praise, had converted some time ago and loved the peace for which he was to die. Clad in the best purple with his own blood, he died not by mistake nor by his own frenzy, but his martyrdom is proven by true piety. Observe the first letters: in them is the name of honor, 'Deacon'.
EDCS-14400008.summary: This inscription records the martyrdom of Nabor, a deacon who was killed during the Donatist schism, emphasizing his conversion and peaceful death.

EDCS-14700093.translation: Sacred to the departed spirits. Lucius Caecilius Silanus lived 18 months.
EDCS-14700093.summary: This is a funerary inscription recording the short life of Lucius Caecilius Silanus, who died at 18 months old.

EDCS-14700094.translation: Sacred to the departed spirits. Antesa Saturnina lived 40 years and 4 months. Sacred to the departed spirits. Aelius Felix lived 66 years.
EDCS-14700094.summary: This inscription is a funerary epitaph recording the lifespans of two individuals, Antesa Saturnina and Aelius Felix.

EDCS-14700095.translation: Sacred to the departed spirits. Caellia Sabina, sweet and dutiful, daughter of Surbacis, lived 20 years, here she is laid to rest.
EDCS-14700095.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for Caellia Sabina, commemorating her life and parentage.

EDCS-14700096.translation: Sacred to the departed spirits. Iunia Saturnina, pure and modest wife of Lucius Antestius, lived 24 years and 8 months, here she is laid to rest.
EDCS-14700096.summary: This funerary inscription honors Iunia Saturnina, describing her as the pure and modest wife of Lucius Antestius.

EDCS-14900001.translation: For Annius Quintus Filius, of the Papirian tribe, Egnatianus, who had discharged all honors, the council, on account of his industry and integrity in administering public business and expenditures in his magistracy, remitted [dues] and dedicated the gifts.
EDCS-14900001.summary: This inscription records a decision by the local council to remit financial obligations for Annius Egnatianus due to his diligent and honest service in his magistracy.

EDCS-14900005.translation: For the Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the second time, by decree of the decurions.
EDCS-14900005.summary: This inscription records a dedication or honor made by the town council (decurions) to Emperor Septimius Severus.

EDCS-14900007.translation: For Lucius Aelius Aurelius Commodus, son of the Emperor Caesar Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Augustus Pius, father of the country, by decree of the decurions, with public money.
EDCS-14900007.summary: This inscription records a dedication or honor made by the town council (decurions) using public funds for Lucius Aelius Aurelius Commodus, son of Antoninus Pius.

EDCS-14900008.translation: With the aqueduct brought, under the administration of Annius Rufus, a most distinguished man, who manages Thysdrus through the Emperor's generosity, supplying the colony and the public squares, and distributing water to cisterns, and granting it to homes under specific conditions, this was dedicated through the provident foresight of a happy age and the inspiration of the powerful Mercury, patron and protector of the colony Thysdrus.
EDCS-14900008.summary: This inscription records the dedication of an aqueduct system in Thysdrus, completed under the administration of Annius Rufus and attributed to divine inspiration.

EDCS-14900009.translation: [Erected by] the soldiers of the Legio III [on behalf of] their Emperor Caesar. [---]
EDCS-14900009.summary: This fragmented inscription likely records a dedication by soldiers of the Legio III to their Emperor Caesar.

EDCS-14900011.translation: Sacred to the departed spirits. Baburia Saturnina. Marcus Caelius Aelianus [erected this] to his most sweet and most fortunate wife. She lived 40 years.
EDCS-14900011.summary: This is a funerary epitaph set up by Marcus Caelius Aelianus for his wife, Baburia Saturnina, noting her lifespan.

EDCS-14900012.translation: Julius Sabinus, lector, lived in peace for 56 years, more or less. Here he is laid to rest.
EDCS-14900012.summary: This funerary inscription records the life and peaceful rest of Julius Sabinus, identified as a 'lector'.

EDCS-14900013.translation: Rosatus Fidelis lived 4 years and 2 months in peace. He was buried on the day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh indiction.
EDCS-14900013.summary: This is a funerary inscription for a child named Rosatus Fidelis, recording his short lifespan and date of burial.

EDCS-14900014.translation: John lies here, from the province of Syria, Apama, faithful in God. He lived in peace for 9 months, buried on the Kalends of January, in the 6th indiction.
EDCS-14900014.summary: This is a funerary inscription for Johannes, who died in Apama, Syria, and was buried on January 1st of the 6th indiction.

EDCS-14900015.translation: Marcus Aemilius Respectus, son of Marcus Aemilius Super, of the Palatina tribe, prefect of the engineers, perpetual priest of the deified Augustus, and his most excellent brother, Marcus Aemilius Respectus, son of Marcus Aemilius, of the Palatina tribe, prefect of the engineers, perpetual priest of the deified Augustus, tribune of the soldiers of the Third Augustan Legion, made this for his most devoted brother after his death.
EDCS-14900015.summary: This funerary monument was erected by Marcus Aemilius Respectus for his brother, Marcus Aemilius Super, who held various priesthoods and military offices.

EDCS-14900016.summary: This is a very brief inscription identifying Theodorus as an archdeacon.

EDCS-14900018.text_edition: \n Lucio Terentio Aquilae Grattiano quaestori provinciae Africae amici ob parem in universos aequitatem et proprium in singulos honorem\n
EDCS-14900018.translation: To Lucius Terentius Aquila Gratianus, quaestor of the province of Africa, from his friends, for his fairness towards all and his particular regard for each individual.
EDCS-14900018.summary: This is a dedication, likely on a monument or statue base, from friends to Lucius Terentius Aquila Gratianus, a quaestor in Africa, honoring his fairness and individual regard.

EDCS-14900019.translation: From Hydatius: To Titus Flavius Umbricius Antistius Saturninus Fortunatianus, a most distinguished man and patron, from Aemilius M[e]sis and his associates.
EDCS-14900019.summary: This is a dedication to Titus Flavius Umbricius Antistius Saturninus Fortunatianus, a distinguished patron, likely from Aemilius M[e]sis and his group.

EDCS-14900020.translation: Of Colonia Iulia Hadrumetina, Publius Icelius Fannius Fortunatus.
EDCS-14900020.summary: This inscription likely records an individual, Publius Icelius Fannius Fortunatus, associated with the colony of Hadrumetum.

EDCS-14900021.translation: Deodatus erected this to the memory of Cassia, his most worthy wife and mother of his sons.
EDCS-14900021.summary: This is a funerary dedication by Deodatus to his wife Cassia, emphasizing her virtues as a spouse and mother.

EDCS-14900022.translation: Norbanus, a boy soldier, lived 19 years.
EDCS-14900022.summary: This is a funerary inscription for Norbanus, a young soldier who died at the age of 19.

EDCS-14900025.translation: Iorticius lived in peace for 65 years, more or less.
EDCS-14900025.summary: This is a funerary inscription for Iorticius, recording his lifespan of approximately 65 years.

EDCS-14900026.text_edition: \n Publio Sulpicio Quirinio Cai Valgio consulibus senatus populusque civitatium stipendiariorum pago Gurzenses hospitium fecerunt quom sic Lucio Domitio Cnaei filio Luci nepoti Ahenobarbo proconsuli eumque et postereis sic eius sibi posterisque sueis sic patronum cooptaverunt isque eos posterosque eorum in fidem clientelamque suam recepit faciundum coeraverunt Ammicar Milchatonis filius Cynasyn Boncar Azzrubalis filius Aethogursensis Muthunbal Saphonis filius Cui Nas Uzitensis\n
EDCS-14900026.translation: In the consulship of Publius Sulpicius Quirinius and Caius Valgius, the senate and people of the allied communities of the Gurzenses district established a guest-friendship with Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, son of Gnaeus, grandson of Lucius, proconsul, and adopted him and his descendants as patron for themselves and their descendants, and he received them and their descendants into his protection and patronage; Ammicar, son of Milchaton; Cynasyn; Boncar, son of Azzrubal; Aethogursensis; Muthunbal, son of Saphon; Cui Nas; Uzitensis undertook its construction.
EDCS-14900026.summary: This inscription records the establishment of a guest-friendship and patronage relationship between the Gurzenses district and the proconsul Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, detailing the agreements and the individuals responsible for its construction.

EDCS-14900027.translation: In the consulship of Aulus Licinius Merva Silianus, the civic community of Gurza from Africa made a treaty of hospitality with Quintus Aufustius Macrinus, son of Gaius, of the Galeria tribe, prefect of the engineers, and they adopted him, his children, and his descendants as their patron, for themselves, their children, and their descendants. Gaius Aufustius Macrinus, son of Gaius, of the Galeria tribe, prefect of the engineers, from Gurza in Africa, received them, their children, and their descendants into his protection and patronage, and that of his successors. The envoys Herennius Maximus, son of Rusticus, and Sempronius Quartus of Iafis, acted in this matter.
EDCS-14900027.summary: This inscription records a hospitality agreement between the city of Gurza and Quintus Aufustius Macrinus, who was also appointed patron.

EDCS-14900029.translation: Victoria for the most unconquered Emperors, by decree of the decurions, with public money.
EDCS-14900029.summary: This inscription records a public dedication or monument erected in honor of the emperors by the town council.

EDCS-14900030.translation: To Lucius Antonius Rogatus, patron of the town council of the Antonia curia, content with this honor, he remitted the money.
EDCS-14900030.summary: This inscription honors Lucius Antonius Rogatus as a patron of the Antonia curia, noting his satisfaction with the honor and his remission of payment.

EDCS-14900031.translation: To Liber Pater Augustus, Salvius Antonius Salvi, exceeding the customary honor, built this altar from the ground up and adorned it with plasterwork and set up a statue of Liber Pater.
EDCS-14900031.summary: This inscription records the construction of an altar and the dedication of a statue to Liber Pater by Salvius Antonius Salvi, who exceeded customary honors.

EDCS-14900032.translation: Of the Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pius Pertinax Augustus Arabicus Adiabenicus Parthicus Maximus.
EDCS-14900032.summary: This is the titulary of Emperor Septimius Severus, likely part of a larger inscription, dating to his reign.

EDCS-14900034.translation: Lucius Antonius Crescens Demetrianus, perpetual priest, in honor of his father's legitimate perpetual priesthood, and 2,000 sesterces, with additional money from his father's decree of the council, made this, in honor of Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Commodus Antoninus Felix Augustus Pius Sarmaticus Germanicus Maximus Britannicus, pontifex maximus, with tribunician power for the 11th time, imperator for the 7th time, consul for the 5th time, father of the fatherland, son of the deified Marcus Aurelius Pius Germanicus Sarmaticus, grandson of the deified Pius, great-grandson of the deified Hadrian, and his great-great-grandson of the deified Trajan Parthicus, and his great-great-great-grandson of the deified Nerva.
EDCS-14900034.summary: This inscription records a dedication by Lucius Antonius Crescens Demetrianus to Emperor Commodus, including a substantial sum of money, likely as part of a public building or honorific monument, dating to Commodus' reign (c. 190-192 AD).

EDCS-14900036.translation: Sacred to the Spirits of the Underworld. Saturnina, an example of marital chastity and piety, who lived chaste for 20 years, 10 months, and 17 days, rests here.
EDCS-14900036.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for Saturnina, recording her age at death and praising her marital virtue, likely dating to the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900037.translation: Sacred to the Spirits of the Underworld. Quintus Iulius Lucanus, son of Medico, to reach my homeland full of joy, I competed for 80 years; now I am quiet here, always with the doctor.
EDCS-14900037.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for Quintus Iulius Lucanus, who apparently lived a long life (80 years) and perhaps served as a doctor or was cared for by one.

EDCS-14900039.summary: This is a very brief funerary epitaph recording the name and age at death of Peregrinus.

EDCS-14900041.translation: Sacred to the Spirits of the Underworld. Quintus Cornelius Arsus, son of Caius, lived 20 years and 10 days. His sons Caius and Quintus made this for their good brother. He is buried here.
EDCS-14900041.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for Quintus Cornelius Arsus, erected by his brothers, dating to the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900042.translation: To the deified Hadrian, founder of the municipality, by decree of the decurions, with public money.
EDCS-14900042.summary: This inscription records a public monument dedicated to the deified Emperor Hadrian, founder of the town, funded by the local council.

EDCS-14900043.translation: To Sextus Cocceius Vibianus, proconsul of the province of Africa, patron of the municipality, by decree of the decurions, with public money.
EDCS-14900043.summary: This inscription records a public monument dedicated to Sextus Cocceius Vibianus, a former proconsul of Africa and patron of the municipality, funded by the local council, likely dating to the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900046.translation: Alexander Severus Augustus [dedicates this] to Jupiter.
EDCS-14900046.summary: This inscription records a dedication by Emperor Alexander Severus to Jupiter, likely part of a temple or altar.

EDCS-14900047.summary: This is the titulary of Emperor Maximinus Thrax, likely part of a larger inscription, dating to his reign.

EDCS-14900048.translation: To Antoninus Pius Augustus Caesar, son of...
EDCS-14900048.summary: This is a fragment of an inscription dedicated to Emperor Antoninus Pius, likely from the 2nd century AD.

EDCS-14900051.summary: This is a very brief, possibly epigrammatic inscription, whose context is unknown but suggests a theme of boldness.

EDCS-14900061.summary: This is a fragmentary inscription mentioning Antoninus, likely referring to a public official, possibly from the Roman imperial period.

EDCS-14900063.translation: To the mother of the camp, the senate...
EDCS-14900063.summary: This inscription fragment likely refers to the deified mother of Emperor Augustus and is related to the senate.

EDCS-14900064.translation: A burial plot was granted by decree of the decurions to Laberia Hostilia Crispinata, daughter of Marcus, wife of Caius Bruttius Praesens, proconsul.
EDCS-14900064.summary: This inscription records the grant of a burial plot to a prominent woman, the wife of a proconsul, by local officials in the 2nd century AD.

EDCS-14900065.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Valgius Secundus, son, decurion of Capsa, lived 30 years. His brother Valgius Datiānus attended to his burial. May your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900065.summary: This is a tombstone inscription for Valgius Secundus, a decurion of Capsa who died at 30, erected by his brother in the Roman imperial period.

EDCS-14900067.translation: Flavia Urbica, mother, made and dedicated this to the perpetual flamen.
EDCS-14900067.summary: This is a dedication made by Flavia Urbica to a perpetual flamen, likely from the Roman imperial period.

EDCS-14900078.translation: Sacred to the departed gods. Gaius Mummius Maximus lived 56 years. May your bones rest well, under the care of Aelius Saturninus. Aelius Saturninus lived 59 years, under the care of [---].
EDCS-14900078.summary: This is a double tombstone inscription recording the ages of Gaius Mummius Maximus and Aelius Saturninus, with a wish for their peaceful rest, and indicating the person who arranged the burials.

EDCS-14900079.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Aelia Saturnina Musica lived 22 years and two months.
EDCS-14900079.summary: This is a tombstone inscription for Aelia Saturnina Musica, who died at age 22, from the Roman imperial period.

EDCS-14900080.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Aelia Fortunata lived 45 years. Caius Iulius Mustus made this for his most sweet wife, because of her merits. Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Aelia Cada lived 31 years. Melita dedicated [this]. Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Iulia Siusiana lived 32 years. Maximus and G. Cottis, citizen, administered [the burial]. Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Iulius Fort [lived] 58 years. May your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900080.summary: This is a complex tomb inscription recording the deaths and burials of several individuals, including Aelia Fortunata, Aelia Cada, Iulia Siusiana, and Iulius Fort, likely from the Roman imperial period.

EDCS-14900081.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Aemilia Musica lived 20 years. Iulius Saturninus lived [years]. Iulius Candidus lived 17 years. Iulia Cara lived [year]. Iulius Pegasus lived 16 years.
EDCS-14900081.summary: This is a tomb inscription listing the ages at death of several individuals, including Aemilia Musica, Iulius Candidus, and Iulius Pegasus, from the Roman imperial period.

EDCS-14900082.translation: Dedicated to the departed spirits. Caius Ann Maxentius lived 81 years. Caius An Maximus lived 32 years.
EDCS-14900082.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespans of two individuals, Caius Ann Maxentius and Caius An Maximus.

EDCS-14900084.translation: Dedicated to the departed spirits. Blandulus, son of Pothus, lived 45 years.
EDCS-14900084.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespan of Blandulus, son of Pothus.

EDCS-14900085.translation: Dedicated to the departed spirits. Monument erected by the living Lucius Caecilius Odianus, son of Clodius, who lived 70 years. His sons oversaw its completion. May your bones rest well, dedicated to the departed spirits. Caecilia ad i. May your bones rest well, dedicated to the departed spirits. Caecilius Felix lived [---] years.
EDCS-14900085.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespan of Lucius Caecilius Odianus, its commissioner, and his sons who completed it, as well as mentioning Caecilia ad i and Caecilius Felix.

EDCS-14900086.translation: Dedicated to the departed spirits. Caius C. Severus lived 28 years, overseen by his father Crispinius. May your bones rest well. Caius Trugetius Salustianus lived 21 years, overseen by his father Crispinius. May your bones rest well. Dedicated to the departed spirits. Dedicated to the departed spirits. [---] bones rest well.
EDCS-14900086.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespans of Caius C. Severus and Caius Trugetius Salustianus, both overseen by their father Crispinius.

EDCS-14900087.translation: Dedicated to the departed spirits. Domitia Caesia Optima, a most chaste woman in life, a matron of the rarest frugality and utmost indulgence, lived 68 years. Her son Iulius Senteanus arranged for the monument to be made. May your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900087.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespan and virtues of Domitia Caesia Optima, for whom her son Iulius Senteanus arranged the monument.

EDCS-14900088.translation: Dedicated to the departed spirits. Caius Fabius Fronto lived 35 years, overseen by his brothers Fabius Rufinus and Felix. May your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900088.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespan of Caius Fabius Fronto, overseen by his brothers Fabius Rufinus and Felix.

EDCS-14900089.translation: [---] lived 80 years, overseen by his son Flavius Citioris. Dedicated to the departed spirits. Flavia Fortunata lived 33 years, strong [---]. Flavius Felix and Flavius Citus, his sons, took care of it.
EDCS-14900089.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespans of an unnamed individual and Flavia Fortunata, with care provided by Flavius Citioris, Flavius Felix, and Flavius Citus.

EDCS-14900091.translation: Flavius Saturninus lived 61 years. Aemilius lived [---] years.
EDCS-14900091.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespans of Flavius Saturninus and Aemilius.

EDCS-14900092.translation: Dedicated to the departed spirits. Flavia Donatilla, wife of Quintianus, lived 33 years. May your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900092.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespan of Flavia Donatilla, wife of Quintianus.

EDCS-14900093.translation: [---] Lucanus lived 75 years. [---] Deus lived 60 years. Iulius Gaudinus lived 50 years.
EDCS-14900093.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespans of three individuals: Lucanus, Deus, and Iulius Gaudinus.

EDCS-14900094.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the underworld. Publius Tannonius Iustus lived 43 years. He is buried here, with Tannoniu Saturninus acting as caretaker. May your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900094.summary: A funerary inscription for Publius Tannonius Iustus, a tombstone erected by Tannoniu Saturninus, dating from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900096.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the underworld. Ulpia Quinta lived 105 years. Her bones rest well. Ulpius Quintasius lived two years, cared for by his paternal uncle.
EDCS-14900096.summary: A funerary inscription for Ulpia Quinta and Ulpius Quintasius, a tombstone erected by a paternal uncle, dating from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900097.translation: naso to his wife, his sister. May your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900097.summary: A fragment of a funerary inscription, likely continuing EDCS-14900096, expressing good wishes for the deceased.

EDCS-14900098.translation: ina lived 77 years, cared for by
EDCS-14900098.summary: A fragment of a funerary inscription, likely continuing EDCS-14900097, recording a person's lifespan and care.

EDCS-14900099.translation: Antonius Africanus, quinquennial magistrate, erected this monument, victorious in war from the founding of the city.
EDCS-14900099.summary: A funerary monument erected by Antonius Africanus, a quinquennial magistrate, celebrating his military victory, likely from the Roman Republican or early Imperial period.

EDCS-14900104.translation: Ispesina lived in peace for months
EDCS-14900104.summary: A funerary inscription fragment recording the lifespan in months of Ispesina, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900106.translation: Urbanilla, my wife, full of modesty, is laid here in Rome, companion of my business, supported by parsimony. After all my achievements were accomplished, when she was returning with me to my homeland, miserable Carthage snatched her from me. Alas, there is no hope of living for me without such a wife, she who used to keep my home, she who used to help me with her counsel. Sadly she rests, enclosed in marble. Lucius, I, her husband, covered you here with marble. Fate gave this lot to us when we were given to Lucius.
EDCS-14900106.summary: A funerary epitaph for Urbanilla, erected by her husband Lucius, lamenting her death in Carthage and praising her virtues as a wife and companion, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900107.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the underworld. Helvia Victoria lived 20 years. Her father and her husband made and dedicated this to her.
EDCS-14900107.summary: A funerary inscription for Helvia Victoria, erected by her father and husband, dating from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900108.summary: A funerary inscription fragment for Aulus Viliuius, recording his lifespan, dating from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900109.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the underworld. Caecilius Privatus lived 78 years.
EDCS-14900109.summary: A funerary inscription for Caecilius Privatus, dating from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900110.summary: This is a funerary epitaph recording the lifespan of Caecilius Privatus Iunior.

EDCS-14900111.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Aemilius Evasius lived for 51 years; may your bones rest well.
EDCS-14900111.summary: This is a funerary epitaph recording the lifespan of Aemilius Evasius, with a wish for peaceful rest.

EDCS-14900115.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Iulius Faustinus lived for 43 years; may your bones rest well.

Rogatus mentioned above made and dedicated this during his lifetime.

EDCS-14900117.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Iulia Galla, who was also called Meduria, lived for 53 years; may your bones rest well.

EDCS-14900119.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Quintus Iunius Rogatus lived for 60 years. Iunius Rogatus Urbanus Quintosus made and dedicated this to his dearest father. Eiafrivia, his sister, lived for 25 years.
EDCS-14900119.summary: This funerary epitaph records the lifespan of Quintus Iunius Rogatus, identifies Iunius Rogatus Urbanus Quintosus as the dedicator to his father, and also records the lifespan of his sister Eiafrivia.

EDCS-14900122.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Simplicius made this monument for himself and his wife; he lived for 56 years.

EDCS-14900123.translation: Sacred to the departed spirits. Their sons Vaterius Donatus and his brother Vaterius Muthunus erected and dedicated this monument. Gaius Vaterius Ianuarius lived [certain number of] years, and his wife Vateria Secunda lived [certain number of] years.

EDCS-14900164.translation: To the colony of Cillium. Quintus Manlius Felix Receptus, son of Caius, of the Papiria tribe, with characteristic generosity towards his fatherland, erected this arch with its insignia. On the occasion of its dedication, he gave gifts of food to the decurions and a feast to the curiae. By the clemency of our lords, the most invincible Emperors Constantine and Licinius, the ornaments of liberty were restored, and the ancient insignia of citizenship, under the administration of Ceionius Apronianus, most distinguished man and patron of the city.
EDCS-14900164.summary: This is a public inscription from Cillium dating to the reign of Constantine and Licinius (early 4th century AD), recording the erection of an arch and restoration of civic honors by Quintus Manlius Felix Receptus.

EDCS-14900165.text_edition: \n Sint licet exiguae fugentia tempora vitae parvaque raptorum cito transeat hora dierum mergat et Elysiis mortalia corpora terris adsidue rupto Lachesis male conscia penso iam tamen inventa est blandae rationis imago per quam prolatos homines in tempora plura longior excipiat memoratio multaque servet secum per titulos mansuris fortius annis ecce recens pietas omni placitura favore ingentem famae numerum cum laude meretur exemplo iam plena novo quam Flavius alto more Secundus agens patrio signavit honore quis non iam pronis animi virtutibus adsit quis non hoc miretur opus fusasque videndo divitias stupeat tantos se cernere census per quos aetherias surgunt monimenta per auras haec est fortunae melius laudanda facultas sic sibi perpetuas faciunt impendia sedes sic immortales scit habere pecunia mores aeterno quotiens stabilis bene figitur usu viderit ille furor nimio qui ducitur auro quem trahit argenti venalis sanguine candor viderit et fusae vanis in amoribus errans gloria luxuriae peregrinas quaerere magno quae didicit vestes gemmasque nitore placentes aut ab Aeruthreo venientia munera fluctu quam laedunt gentes vario certamine rerum Graecia cum pueris Hispania Pallados usu venatu Lybiae tellus orientis amomo Aegyptos Phariis levitatibus artibus actis Gallia semper ovans dives Campania vino haec cito deficiunt et habent breve munus amoris momentis damnata suis sed si quis ad omnes respiciat vitae casus hominemque laboret metiri brevitate sua tunc credere discet nil aliut sic melius fieri nisi viribus aevi quot sic possit durare diu sub honore deorum nunc ego non dubitem tacitis Acherontos in umbris si post Fata manent sensus gaudere parentem saepe Secunde tuum reliquas et spernere turmas quod sciat hic tantam faciem superesse sepulchri perpetua novitate sui sic stare nitentes consensus lapidum sic de radice levatos in melius crevisse gradus ut et angulus omnis sic quasi mollitae ductus sit stamine cerae mobilibus signis hilaris scalptura novatur et licet atsidue sic probet hos vaga turba decores lucentes stupeat pariter pendere columnas quit sic cum militiae titulos ipsumque parentem numinibus dederis haec gaudia saepe videntem quae quondam dedit ipse loco dum munera Bacchi multa creat primasque cupit componere vites et nemus exornat revocatis saepius undis permittant mihi fata loqui noctisque timendae regnator Stygius sic immortalis haberi iam debet pater ecce tuus Ditisque relicti tristem deservisse domum dum tempore toto mavolt sic haec monumenta sequi scriptisque per aevom vivere nominibus solitis insistere lucis adsidue patrias hinc cernere dulciter arces quosque dedit natis prope semper habere Penates forsitan haec multi vano sermone ferentes venturae citius dicant praesagia mortis si quis dum vivit ponat monimenta sic futuris temporibus mihi non tales sunt pectore sensus set sic puto securos fieri quicumque parare aeternam volvere domum certoque rigore numquam lapsuros vitae defigere muros fatis certa via est neque se per stamina mutat Atropos ut primo coepit decurrere filo crede Secunde mihi pensatos ibis in annos set sic securus eris set sic toto pectore dives dum nulli gravis esse potes nec plena labore testamenta facis tuus hoc dum non timet heres ut sic aedificet iam nunc quodcumque relinques totum perveniet tua quo volet ire voluntas sed revocat me cura operis celsique decores stat sublimis honor vicinaque nubila pulsat et solis metitur iter si iungere montes forte velint oculi vincuntur in ordine colles si videas campos infra iacet abdita tellus non sic Romuleas exire colossos in arces dicitur aut circi medias obeliscus in auras nec sic sistrigeri demonstrat pervia Nili dum sua perspicuis aperit Pharos aequora flammis quid non docta facit pietas lapis ecce foratus luminibus multis hortatur currere blandas intus apes et cerineos componere nidos ut semper domus haec Thymbraeo nectare dulcis sudet florisapos dum dant nova mella liquores huc iterum pietas venerandas erige mentes et mea quo nosti carmina more fove ecce Secundus adest iterum qui pectore sancto non monimenta patri sed nova templa dedit quo nunc Calliope gemino me limite cogis quas iam transegi rursus adire vias nempe fuit nobis operis descriptio magni diximus et iunctis saxa polita locis circuitus nemorum currentes dulciter undas atque sic reportantes mella frequenter apes hoc tamen hoc solum nostrae puto defuit arti dum cadis ad multos ebria Musa iocos in summo tremulas galli non diximus alas altior extrema qui puto nube volat cuius si membris vocem EDCS-14900165.translation: Though life's fleeting moments be brief, and the hour of swift days pass quickly, and though the body sinks to the Elysian fields, and Lachesis incessantly, unaware, snaps the unjust thread, yet now an image of gentle reason has been found, through which those men, granted longer time, might be received into future eras, and much might be preserved within, stronger than years through lasting inscriptions. Behold, a recent piety, pleasing to all with favor, earns immense fame and praise through a new example, which Flavius Secundus, following his father's custom, has marked with honor. Who would not then incline to his noble virtues? Who would not admire this work and, seeing the poured-out wealth, marvel at such fortunes by which monuments rise to the heavens through the air? This is fortune's faculty, better to be praised, thus they make eternal seats for themselves, thus money knows how to have immortal qualities, whenever it is firmly fixed to eternal use. Let him see that madness which is led by excessive gold, let him see that which is drawn by the venal brightness of silver, let him see and the glory of luxury, wandering in vain loves, seeking foreign garments and gems shining with brilliance, or gifts from the Erythraean waves, how they harm nations in varied competition of affairs: Greece with its boys, Spain with its use of Pallas, Libya with its hunting, the East with its perfume, Egypt with its fleeting tricks, Gaul always rejoicing, wealthy Campania with wine. These quickly pass and have a brief reward of love, condemned by moments. But if anyone looks at the chances of life and labors to measure man by his brevity, then he will learn that nothing else is so well done as to endure through the forces of age. Whoever can last so long under the honor of the gods. Now I shall not doubt, in the silent shades of Acheron, if feeling remains after death, that your father, Secundus, rejoices and scorns the other crowds, knowing that such a splendor of tomb survives through its perpetual novelty, that the gleaming stones stand thus, raised from their foundation, that the steps have grown better, as if every corner were shaped from softened wax, and is renewed by mobile designs and cheerful carving. And although the wandering crowd may constantly approve these ornaments, marvel at the shining columns, yet you, Secundus, when you give these honors to the gods, you will often see these joys, which he himself once gave, creating many gifts of Bacchus, arranging vines, and adorning the grove with frequently recalled waters. May the fates permit me to speak, and may the ruler of the dreaded night and Stygian realm grant that your father may now be considered immortal. Behold, he has left the sad home of Dis, preferring throughout all time to follow these monuments and live through inscriptions for the ages, to stand by familiar names, to see his ancestral citadels with delight, and to always have near him the Penates granted to his children. Perhaps many, speaking vainly, will call these omens of approaching death, if someone erects monuments while alive. But I have no such feelings in my heart; rather, I think that whoever prepares to build an eternal home and, with certain rigor, to establish walls of life that will never fall, becomes secure. Fate has a certain path and Atropos does not change herself through the threads. Believe me, Secundus, you will go into calculated years, but you will be secure and rich in heart, as long as you can displease no one and make your wills not full of labor, so that your heir does not fear that whatever you leave will be built. Everything will go where you wish your will to go. But the care of the work calls me back, and the lofty adornments. The honor stands sublimely, touching the neighboring clouds, and measures the sun's course. If eyes wished to join the mountains, the hills are overcome in order. If you see the plains, the earth below lies hidden. Not thus do the colossal structures of Rome emerge into citadels, nor does the obelisk in the center of the Circus reach the sky, nor does the lighthouse of the Nile, while revealing the seas with its clear flames, show the way. What does learned piety not achieve? Behold, this stone, pierced with many lights, urges bees to run inside and arrange their honeycombs, so that this house may always flow sweet with Thymbraean nectar, while flowers give new honeyed liquids. Here again, piety, lift your venerable minds, and foster my songs in the familiar way. Behold, Secundus is here again, who in his holy heart gave not monuments to his father, but new temples. To which path do you, Calliope, compel me now to return with a double path? Indeed, we described a great work, and polished stones joined in places, surrounding groves, flowing waters, and bees frequently carrying honey. Yet, I think only this was missing from my art, while my drunken Muse indulged in many jests; we did not describe the trembling wings of the hawk on the summit, which, I think, flies above the highest cloud, whose voice, if nature had given it limbs, would compel all the gods to rise in the morning. And now the thresholds are marked with names, and credulous life is discerned by its own titles. I wish you, Secundus, to live many happy years, and to read the monuments you have made. Titus Flavius Secundus, son, made this for his pious father Titus Flavius Secundus, who served in the army for 33 years and lived 110 years; he lies here. For his pious mother Flavia Urbana, who lived 105 years; she lies here. For his pious sister Flavia Secunda, who lived 20 years; she lies here. For his pious brother Titus Flavius Marcellus, who served in the army for 12 years and lived 35 years; he lies here. For his pious sister Flavia Sperata, who lived 36 years; she lies here. For his pious wife, the perpetual flamninica, Aemilia Pacata, daughter of Sextus, who lived 53 years; she lies here. Titus Flavius Secundus Papirius, himself perpetual flamen, lived 60 years; he lies here. For Flavia Pacata, daughter of Titus, perpetual flamninica of the colony of Thelepte, a pious daughter; Flavia Libera, mother, erected the statue; she lived 15 years and 10 months; she lies here. Flavia Libera, wife of Titus Flavius Secundus, a pious woman, lived 88 years; she lies here. Flavia Faustina, a pious woman, lived 38 years; she lies here. Titus Flavius Faustinus and Flavia Victoria, parents, erected this. Flavia Libera, a pious woman, lived 16 years and 6 months; Titus Flavius Faustinus and Flavia Victoria, parents, erected this; she lies here. Titus Flavius Papirius Receptus, of the aediles' rank, quaestor of the treasury, decurion of the colony of Thelepte, a pious man, lived 36 years; he lies here. Titus Flavius Faustinus and Flavia Victoria, parents, erected this.
EDCS-14900165.summary: This extensive funerary monument commemorates multiple members of the Flavius Secundus family, including the father, son (who likely commissioned the monument), wife, siblings, and children, detailing their lives, military service, and religious offices, with elaborate verses praising the piety and legacy of the family, especially Titus Flavius Secundus.

EDCS-14900166.translation: Though life's fleeting moments may be brief, and the swift hour of snatched days soon pass, and though the infernal Lachesis, with malevolent, ignorant hand, drags mortal bodies to the Elysian fields, yet now an image of gentle reason has been found, through which men, drawn forth, may receive a longer remembrance for many more years, and keep many things with them through inscriptions, more steadfastly than passing years. Behold, a recent piety, pleasing to all with favor, merits a great number of fame with praise, following a new example. For Flavius Secundus, acting with high honor from his father, has marked this. Who would not attend to such virtues of the soul? Who would not admire this work and, seeing the poured-out riches, envy so great a fortune, through which monuments rise to the heavens through the air? This is fortune's faculty, to be praised the more, thus they make eternal seats for themselves. Thus money knows how to have immortal ways, whenever it is steadfastly and well established in use. Let him see that frenzy driven by excessive gold, and that desire for silver's venal brightness, and that glory of luxury wandering in vain loves, seeking foreign garments and jewels pleasing with their glitter, or gifts coming from the Erythraean waves, and the lands that harm nations with varied competition: Greece with its boys, Spain with its use of Pallas, Libya with its hunting, the East with its amomum, Egypt with its shallow arts from the Pharos, Gaul always rejoicing, Campania with its wine. These things quickly fail and have a brief purpose, condemned by the moments of custom. But if anyone looks at all the chances of life and tries to measure man by his brevity, then he will learn to believe that nothing better can be done than to possess a lifetime that can endure for a long time under the honor of the gods. Now I will not hesitate, in the silent shades of Acheron, if sense remains after death, to rejoice that your father, Secundus, often enjoys this and scorns the remaining crowds, because he knows that such a magnificent tomb remains, renewed by its perpetual novelty, the stones thus standing, raised from their roots, the steps having grown better, so that every corner seems to have been drawn with soft wax, and the sculpture is enlivened by moving signs. And though the wandering crowd always approves of these, and admires the shining columns and the honors, and the titles of military service, and if you yourself have given these joys to your parents, who once gave him these things while pouring out Bacchic offerings and wishing to arrange the first vines, and he often adorns the grove with renewed waters. May the fates permit me to speak. May the ruler of the Stygian night thus be immortal. Behold, your father, rich and left behind, has sadly forsaken his home, while for all time he prefers to follow these monuments and live through writings for ages, to stand on familiar thresholds of light, and to see his ancestral citadels from here with delight, and to always have the Penates given to his children nearby. Perhaps many, speaking in vain, will call these omens of future death, if anyone erects monuments for future times while alive. But I do not have such feelings in my heart. Rather, I believe that those who prepare an eternal home and fix the walls of life with certain rigor, never to falter, become secure. There is a certain path for fate, and Atropos does not change it with her threads as she began to unwind the first spool. Believe me, Secundus, you will go into calculated years, but you will be secure, and rich in spirit, as long as you can be burdensome to no one and do not make wills full of trouble. As long as your heir does not fear this, that whatever you leave now, he will build in such a way, all will reach where you wish it to go. But the care of the lofty work calls me back, and its decorations. The honor stands sublimely, touching the nearby clouds, and measures the sun's journey. If eyes should wish to join mountains, hills are conquered in order. If you see fields, the earth lies below. Not thus do the colossal structures emerge from Rome into its citadels, nor does the obelisk rise into the middle of the Circus into the air, nor does the Pharos on the Nile show the way through its perpetual flames, opening the waters. What does not learned piety achieve? Behold, this stone speaks with many lights, urging the gentle bees within to run and arrange their waxen nests, so that this house may always sweat with thyme-scented nectar, and the flowers give new liquid honey.
EDCS-14900166.summary: This is a long, complex funerary poem in Latin elegiac couplets, likely from the late Roman Empire, commemorating a monument erected by Flavius Secundus for his father, praising the enduring nature of a well-built monument and the legacy it provides, contrasting it with the transience of material wealth and worldly pleasures.

EDCS-14900167.translation: Come hither again, piety, and lift your minds to venerate, and foster my verses in your accustomed way. Behold, Secundus is here again, who with a holy heart has dedicated not monuments to his father, but new temples. To which path do you, Calliope, compel me again to tread? For indeed, we had a description of a great work: we spoke of polished stones joined in places, circuits of groves, and streams flowing sweetly, and bees frequently bringing back honey. Yet, I think, only this was missing from our art, while many Muses, drunk with jokes, have celebrated the trembling wings of the rooster that flies higher than the highest cloud, whose voice, if nature had given it to his limbs, would compel all the gods to rise in the morning. And now the thresholds are marked with certain names, and a credulous life is seen in its inscriptions. I wish, Secundus, that you may live many years happily, and may you read the monuments you have made.
EDCS-14900167.summary: This is a Latin poem, likely from the late Roman Empire, accompanying a monument possibly associated with a temple or religious structure, commissioned by Secundus and addressed to the Muse Calliope, celebrating the artistic and religious significance of the work.

EDCS-14900168.translation: Flavia Faustina, dutiful, lived 38 years. She is buried here. Titus Flavius Faustinus and Flavia Victoria placed [this monument].
EDCS-14900168.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for Flavia Faustina, who died at the age of 38, erected by her parents, Titus Flavius Faustinus and Flavia Victoria, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-14900169.translation: Flavia Libera, dutiful, lived 16 years and 6 months. Titus Flavius Faustinus and Flavia Victoria, her parents, set this up. She rests here.
EDCS-14900169.summary: A tombstone recording the short life of Flavia Libera, set up by her parents.

EDCS-14900170.translation: Titus Flavius Papiria Receptus, formerly aedile and quaestor of the treasury, a decurion of the colony of Thelepte, dutiful, lived 36 years. He rests here. Titus Flavius Faustinus and Flavia Victoria, his parents, set this up.
EDCS-14900170.summary: A tombstone for Titus Flavius Papiria Receptus, a local official, set up by his parents.

EDCS-14900171.translation: Marcus Petronius Fortunatus served for 4 years in the I Italica Legion as a record-keeper, a dispatch runner, a junior officer, a standard-bearer, and a centurion appointed by the legion's vote. He served as centurion in the I Italica Legion, the VII Legion, the I Minervia Legion, the X Gemina Legion, the II Augusta Legion, the III Gallica Legion, the XXX Ulpia Legion, the VI Victrix Legion, the III Cyrenaica Legion, the XV Apollinaris Legion, the II Parthica Legion, and the I Adiutrix Legion. He achieved the rank of centurion through valor in the Parthian campaign, winning a mural crown, torcs, and phalerae. He lived 80 years until the completion of the work. For himself and for his dearest wife Claudia Marcia Capitoina, who lived 65 years until the completion of the work. And for his son Marcus Petronius Fortunatus, he served for 6 years as centurion in the XXII Primigenia Legion and as centurion in the II Augusta Legion. He lived 35 years. For whom Fortunatus and Marcia, his dearest parents, made this memorial.
EDCS-14900171.summary: A detailed tombstone for Marcus Petronius Fortunatus, chronicling his extensive military career and awards, and also commemorating his wife and son.

EDCS-14900173.translation: Sacred to the shades of the departed. Flavius Certus, chief magistrate, quinquennial official, lived 29 years. [--- illegible ---] his dear [--- illegible ---]
EDCS-14900173.summary: A tombstone for Flavius Certus, a local magistrate, possibly with other illegible text.

EDCS-14900175.translation: Sacred to the shades of the departed. Marcus Pontius Datus the Younger lived [--- illegible ---]. Sacred to the shades of the departed. Pontius Secundianus, dutiful, lived 27 years. Pontius Datus, their father, took care of it. Sacred to the shades of the departed. Sentia Extricata lived 65 years. Sacred to the shades of the departed. Pontia Faustina, dutiful, lived 18 years.
EDCS-14900175.summary: A tombstone with multiple entries, likely commemorating several family members: Marcus Pontius Datus the Younger, Pontius Secundianus, Sentia Extricata, and Pontia Faustina, arranged by Pontius Datus.

EDCS-14900176.translation: [---] lived 47 years. May her ashes rest here. Her husband So orius Secundus.
EDCS-14900176.summary: A tombstone recording the death of a woman, set up by her husband.

EDCS-14900177.translation: Rocna Birzilis, daughter, dutiful, lived 40 years. Her husband Masul took care of it. She rests here.
EDCS-14900177.summary: A tombstone for Rocna Birzilis, set up by her husband.

EDCS-14900183.translation: To Marcus Aelius Aurelius Verus Caesar, consul for the second time, son of Imperator Caesar Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Augustus Pius, father of the fatherland, by decree of the decurions, with public funds.
EDCS-14900183.summary: A dedication, likely for a public building or monument, to Marcus Aurelius Verus Caesar.

EDCS-14900185.translation: To the Emperor Caesar Lucius Domitius Alexander, pious, fortunate, invincible, ever Augustus.
EDCS-14900185.summary: An acclamation or dedication to Emperor Caracalla (Lucius Domitius Alexander).

EDCS-14900188.translation: Emperor Caesar Augustus. The Sufetulensians built this, and by decree of the decurions, with public funds.
EDCS-14900188.summary: A dedication by the inhabitants of Sufetula for a public work funded by the community and approved by its council.

EDCS-14900189.translation: Tianus and Va Festus and Va tium
EDCS-14900189.summary: This inscription appears to be a fragmented dedication or funerary text mentioning several personal names.

EDCS-14900191.translation: Isidora, daughter of AIISO, and Pan s
EDCS-14900191.summary: This inscription is a fragmented funerary dedication mentioning the names Isidora and Pan s, likely related to a tomb.

EDCS-14900194.translation: To Marcus Cornelius Linarius, proconsul, for the Republic of Rome, on account of his piety and obedience, by decree of the decurions, with public money.
EDCS-14900194.summary: This is a public monument erected by decree of the decurions with public funds to honor Marcus Cornelius Linarius, proconsul, for his piety and obedience, likely from the Roman Republic period.

EDCS-14900195.translation: To Flavia Statianilla, of most illustrious memory, grandmother, as an example of utmost piety, by Lucius Servaeus Amicus Potitianus, vir clarissimus, her grandson.
EDCS-14900195.summary: This funerary inscription honors Flavia Statianilla, a grandmother of noble status, as a model of piety, dedicated by her grandson Lucius Servaeus Amicus Potitianus.

EDCS-14900196.translation: To Servaea Novella Rufina Potitiana, a woman of most illustrious memory, by her freedmen Servaeus Eugenius and Vagulus.
EDCS-14900196.summary: This funerary inscription honors Servaea Novella Rufina Potitiana, a woman of high status, and was dedicated by her freedmen Servaeus Eugenius and Vagulus.

EDCS-14900197.translation: To Servaea Flavia Statianilla Valeriana, a most illustrious girl, by her freedmen Servaeus Eugenius and Vagulus.
EDCS-14900197.summary: This funerary inscription honors Servaea Flavia Statianilla Valeriana, a young girl of high status, and was dedicated by her freedmen Servaeus Eugenius and Vagulus.

EDCS-14900198.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Iunia Passeniana, mother, made this for Quintus Turranius Natalis Censorinus, Roman knight.
EDCS-14900198.summary: This is a funerary dedication ('Dis Manibus sacrum') for Quintus Turranius Natalis Censorinus, a Roman knight, made by his mother Iunia Passeniana.

EDCS-14900199.translation: To Quintus Fabius Saturninus Honoratianus, priest of the ancestral gods, for his blameless conduct in both magistracies, by the Flavian curia of all.
EDCS-14900199.summary: This inscription honors Quintus Fabius Saturninus Honoratianus, a priest, for his good conduct in his two magistracies, dedicated by the Flavian curia.

EDCS-14900200.translation: Marcellus, a noble doctor by art, rests here. He lived for almost thirty-two years, but when he had prepared everything to please with his gifts, consumed by a strong fever, he died.
EDCS-14900200.summary: This is a tombstone for Marcellus, a respected doctor who died at the age of thirty-two after preparing to offer his gifts.

EDCS-14900243.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Aemilius Donatus, aged eight years, one month, and seven days, and two hours, rests here.
EDCS-14900243.summary: This is a funerary inscription ('Dis Manibus sacrum') recording the death of Aemilius Donatus at the age of eight years, one month, seven days, and two hours.

EDCS-14900244.translation: Marcus Aurelius the shipowner lived 72 years, 6 months, and 16 days.
EDCS-14900244.summary: This inscription records the lifespan of Marcus Aurelius, identified as a shipowner (naurius), likely from a funerary monument.

EDCS-14900245.translation: Sacred to the Spirits of the Dead. Aurelia III Cora lived 51 years.
EDCS-14900245.summary: This is a funerary inscription for Aurelia III Cora, dedicating the monument to the gods of the underworld and recording her lifespan.

EDCS-14900246.translation: To Lucius Turranius Gratianus Crispinus Lucilianus, his patron. Septimius, his freedman.
EDCS-14900246.summary: This inscription is a dedication by a freedman, Septimius, to his patron, Lucius Turranius Gratianus Crispinus Lucilianus.

EDCS-14900247.summary: This is a dedication to Lucius Julius Ievius, likely by an individual or group who donated something, possibly a statue or a building.

EDCS-14900248.translation: The Father dedicates Juno on high and places her in Pompeii, and believed this would be a solace for sorrows and tears, a pause for weeping, but now, by constantly seeing her, he renews both weeping and groaning for Gallus.
EDCS-14900248.summary: This poetic inscription records the dedication of a statue of Juno by a father to alleviate grief, but ironically, its presence causes continued sorrow for Gallus.

EDCS-14900249.summary: This is a fragmented funerary inscription recording the lifespan of Prima, who lived for an unspecified number of years.

EDCS-14900250.summary: This is a fragmentary inscription likely related to the imperial period of Diocletian and Maximian, possibly a dedication or a record of an event.

EDCS-14900252.summary: This is a fragmented funerary inscription recording the lifespan of an individual who lived 75 years.

EDCS-14900256.summary: This is a fragmentary inscription mentioning "Augustus" and Aurelia Sufetana, possibly related to an imperial dedication or a civic honor.

EDCS-14900260.translation: The most splendid and fortunate town council of the colony of Sufetana to Publius Magnus Amandus, perpetual flamen, who was enrolled among the quinquennales. Furthermore, in addition to the full honorarium for the perpetual flaminates and the quinquennality, he offered more than 50,000 sesterces. From the interest of this sum, distributions are given to the decurions every year on the 12th day before the Kalends of November, on the birthday of the god. Quintus Magnius Maximus Flavianus, his son, a Roman knight, content with the honor, made this at his own expense and gave feast-money upon its dedication. The site was granted by decree of the decurions.
EDCS-14900260.summary: This inscription records the endowment of a perpetual priesthood and other honors in the colony of Sufetana by Publius Magnus Amandus, with his son Quintus Magnius Maximus Flavianus fulfilling the dedication of the monument and associated distributions.

EDCS-14900262.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the underworld. Longinia Castula lived for 28 years.
EDCS-14900262.summary: This is a funerary inscription recording the lifespan of Longinia Castula.

EDCS-14900264.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the underworld. Gaius Sta... and his brother Sta... his slave (?)
EDCS-14900264.summary: This is a fragmentary funerary inscription, likely recording names of the deceased and perhaps a relationship or status.

EDCS-14900265.translation: A brother of the rarest character, pious, lived for 35 years and 47 days.
EDCS-14900265.summary: This funerary inscription commemorates a pious brother who lived for 35 years and 47 days.
