EDCS-34100184.translation: Frenalius the Hunter, Exsuperus the Augur, Volens, Sidereus, Atonitus, Beronica, Crysiphus, Sidereus, Igneus, Turinus, Martius, Rapidus, Arminius the Impulser, Castalius, Gelos, Piropus, Euginis the Animator, Bladus, Sidonius, the Omnipotent, Aquila, Licius, Amazonius, Imber, I invoke you, daemon, who dwells here, I hand over to you these horses that you may detain them and entangle them so they cannot move themselves. [In Greek and Latin, invoking a daemon to bind horses].
EDCS-34100184.summary: This is a magical text invoking a daemon to bind horses, likely intended for a chariot race or a similar equestrian event, featuring a long list of proper names and magical formulae.

EDCS-34100185.translation: Just as your stomachs are bound, so let the arms, heart, and senses of Concordius OMATE be bound, together with Karkidon, together with Concordius, and with Alumninus and Pyro Popyiro, with Lascouvus, Bates, and Luciferus Concordius Serenus may he seize them. Just as your feet are bound, so let the feet of Salbius be bound, let the feet of Alumninus and Pyro Poeliarce and Lascouvus be bound, let the feet of OTINOS be bound so that they may be overwhelmed. Bind the feet of Bates and Luciferus and...
EDCS-34100185.summary: This is a magical binding spell (defixio) intended to immobilize or incapacitate several individuals, likely in a competitive context.

EDCS-34100186.translation: I adjure you, holy one, by the living god, to make Tziolus, whom Restuta bore, and Tzelica, the attendant, and Adesicla, whom Victoria bore, defeated, overcome, exhausted, exiled, plundered, beaten, bound, and entangled, and I hand you over Adesicla, whom Victoria bore, falsely, there Adesicla, whom Victoria bore, make them come out wounded, bloody from the amphitheater on the day of the games, the sons of Aemilianus, the day before the Ides of January or the Ides. Go, go, now, now, quickly, quickly! Now, now, quickly, quickly!
EDCS-34100186.summary: This is a magical curse text, likely related to gladiatorial combat or spectacles, seeking the defeat and injury of specific individuals, invoking deities and a set date.

EDCS-34100187.translation: [In Greek and Latin] I adjure you, whoever you are, O demonic spirit, concerning these boundaries, concerning the bear that Viktoría placed there, concerning Tzeiolus whom Restuta placed, concerning Victoria, concerning the friendship and body, may they not be stiff, may they not stand, may they be bound in the depths, sitting on the rock, whose name is true... bind them, tie them together, may they not be able to hunt, to see, to hold, nor may they be able to... I adjure the bear, namely Tziolus, holding the crown, the attendant, and Adesiola whom Victoria bore.
EDCS-34100187.summary: This is a bilingual magical text (Greek and Latin) invoking a daemon to bind or disable individuals and possibly animals (bears), linked to specific people and possibly a ritual object.

EDCS-34100188.translation: Bachachuch, who are in Egypt, great daemon, bind, bind tightly Maurossus the hunter, whom Felicitas bore. Iekri, take away his sleep, may he not sleep. Maurossus, whom Felicitas bore. Parpaxin, almighty god, bring him to the infernal abodes. Maurossus, whom Felicitas bore. Noctukit, who possess the regions of Italy and Campania, who are the region through the Acherusian lake, lead him to the Tartarean abodes within seven days, lead him to the Tartarean abodes. Maurossus, whom Felicitas bore. Butubach, daemon, who possess Spain and Africa, who alone cross the sea, cross over the soul and spirit of Maurossus, whom Felicitas bore. Cross over every remedy and every protective amulet and every safeguard and every libatory oil and bring them, bind them, bind them tightly, consume them, take them away, destroy them, the heart, the limbs, the internal organs of Maurossus, whom Felicitas bore. And I adjure you, whoever is in the underworld, by these holy names of necessity: Maskellei, Maskello, Phnoukentabaoth, Oreobarzagrha, Rheixithon, Hippokton, Pyrktonphit, It H O R Kerderosandalé, Katanekandale, seize him and make him pale, mixed, sad, mute, not in control of himself, Maurossus, whom Felicitas bore. In every combat, in every contest, let him vanish, fall. [Latin text continues with further curses against Maurossus].
EDCS-34100188.summary: This is a complex magical text (a defixio) invoking multiple daemons and divine names to curse and incapacitate a hunter named Maurossus, likely for a gladiatorial or hunting spectacle, detailing various bindings and debilitating effects.

EDCS-34100189.translation: I adjure you, souls of this place, by these holy names Psarchyrin, Oncrobrotescirvio, Arcadams. I adjure you again, souls of this place, Erexcipte, Araracarara, Eptisicere, Cycbacyc, Bacacicyc, Bacaicyc, Obriimmao, Saum, Obriulem, Patatnach, Apomspsesro, Iao, Iosef, Ioerbet, Iopacerbet, Bolcoset, bring destruction to these hunters: Metretes, Syndicius, Celsanus, Atsurius, Felicus, Cardarius, Vincentius, so that they cannot please with their strength. I adjure you by the names heard, O I adjure you by these names of necessity: Temaé, Cerciel, Baciel, Aichecese, Amestubal, Merteme, Perturacrini, Mascelli, Maschello, Phnycentabaot, Zosagrac. And by the great Chaos, I adjure you Iabezepat, Erexcipte, Araracarara, Eptisicere, commanding you and the kings of demons, Bacaxhicyxhdemenon, Bacachicych, commanding you and the judges of bloodless souls who judged you in the swiftness of life, Crinyarincbor, commanding you and the holy god Mercury of the underworld, commanding it, let it be done, dexcocemri. Bind these hunters.
EDCS-34100189.summary: This is a magical curse text (defixio) directed at hunters, invoking various spirits, daemons, and divine names to bring about their destruction and incapacitation, likely related to arena contests.

EDCS-34100190.translation: [In Greek and Latin] ...Vincentius Tiaritio in the amphitheater of Carthage on the day of Mercury, in two, five, in three, nine, to Vincentius Tiaritioni, whom Concordia bore, so that he cannot bind bears in every hour, in every moment, on the day of Mercury. And the strength, the power, the heart, the liver, the mind, the wits, I adjure you, ananamehgisichei, your kingdom, to Vincentius Tiaritioni, whom Concordia bore, in the amphitheater of Carthage on the day of Mercury, bind, entangle Vincentius Tiaritioni, so that he cannot bind bears, may he lose every bear, may Vincentius not be able to kill every bear on the day of Mercury. Now, now, quickly, quickly! Make it so! [Followed by extensive magical formulae and invocations]. I call upon you, the great and powerful one, who holds and binds and possesses with unbreakable, eternal, adamantine chains, and every soul, seize, bind, subject, incline to Vincentius Tiaritioni, whom Concordia bore. Bind Vincentius Tiaritioni in the amphitheater on the day of Mercury. Exterminate Tiaritioni, may he not go out, may he not go out into this place, nor may he go out the gate, nor may he depart from the place, but may he remain in your unbreakable, eternal, adamantine chains. The soul of Vincentius Tiaritioni, whom Concordia bore. Bind, entangle Vincentius Tiaritioni, in two, five, in three, may he be bound, wounded, disabled, may he not be able to run, Vincentius Tiaritioni. Make Vincentius Tiaritioni, Vincentius Tiaritioni in the amphitheater of Carthage. Bind, entangle Vincentius Tiaritioni, in two, five, in three, nine, may he not be able, may he be able on the day of Mercury, so that his soul may not be conquered in battle, may he fail in every hour. Through the spiritual regions...
EDCS-34100190.summary: This is a powerful magical curse text (defixio) directed at a gladiator named Vincentius Tiaritioni, intended to incapacitate him in arena contests, especially against bears, invoking numerous daemonic names and divine powers.

EDCS-34100202.translation: O Semiramis, Iao, Ao, Baubo, Ehaehie, Sophosan, Kanthara, Ereshigal, Sankiste, Dodekakete, Akrourobore, Kothire, Dropide, Tartarouke, Anoch, Anoch, Katabreimō, the terrible, that you may conquer the enemies; Damastrei, you, the great goddess, I commend to Seruabios, because he cursed the parturient. Run, all of you, and infernal demons, bind those horses' feet so that they cannot run, those horses whose names you have here written and entrusted: Inpletus, Nitidus, Patricius, Nauta, Sium, A, Tacharchē. Bind them so they cannot run in tomorrow's and the day after tomorrow's races, Patricius Nitidus Nauta Inpletus Tacharchē. And the lady Campana, Kampteras, Nitidus Patricius Nauta Inpletus Tacharchē, so that they cannot run tomorrow and the day after and at all hours in the circus, may they fall as you have deservedly fallen, Bios Thanatos. Now, now, quickly, quickly, because the Syphonian demons lead them.
EDCS-34100202.summary: This is a magical curse text, likely from a defixio or curse tablet, written in a mixture of Greek and Latin, invoking deities and demons to cripple horses in races and harm individuals.

EDCS-34100205.translation: Baitmos, Arbittos, Lynceus, Margarita, press them down, pull them down, kill them, in the fifth pulling down, sever their nerves, cut their sinews, so that they may not have breath. I adjure you, demon, whoever you are, and I demand of you from this hour and from this moment that the horses you have with you be tormented. By Donatus, founder of the Prasini, I adjure you by him who released you from the bonds of life, O highest sea, air, and celestial god.
EDCS-34100205.summary: This is a magical curse text, likely a defixio, where the dedicator implores a demon to torment and kill horses belonging to rivals, possibly in a chariot race, invoking divine and demonic powers.

EDCS-34100444.summary: This is a fragment of a magical curse text, possibly a defixio, with illegible portions, indicating a curse to sever nerves and inflict harm.

EDCS-34100445.translation: To Cuigeu, Censeu, Cimbeu, Perfleu, Diarunco, Deasta, Bescu, Berebescu, Arurara, Baazagra, and to the ruler of the underworld, and to you, I beg that you remove from them the nerves, strength, marrow, and impulses of victory. Do not scorn my words, but let these names listed below move you, and them, and these horses to run for me, by these holy names of necessity.
EDCS-34100445.summary: This is a magical curse text, likely a defixio, where the dedicator lists names and invokes underworld deities to sap the strength and victory from opposing horses and their owners.

EDCS-34100448.translation: I adjure you, demon, whoever you are, and I demand of you from this day, from this hour, from this moment, that ... be tormented ... I adjure you, demon, whoever you are, and I demand of you that ... be tormented ... by the sea, air, and highest god. Iao, ou, iaaaaoooo, ia.
EDCS-34100448.summary: This is a fragment of a magical curse text, possibly a defixio, where a demon is adjured to torment individuals or entities, invoking powerful deities and divine names.

EDCS-34100449.translation: Quinto Ocuria, anochoton, barnion, formione, efecebul. I adjure you, whoever you are, and I demand of you from this day, from this hour, from this moment, that ... be tormented. I adjure you by him who released you from the bonds of life, O highest sea, air, and celestial god. I adjure you to take these horses ...
EDCS-34100449.summary: This is a magical curse text, likely a defixio, where the dedicator adjures a demon to torment someone or something and to deliver horses, invoking divine powers.

EDCS-34100450.translation: Ocuria, anoch oton, barnion, formione, efecebul. I adjure you, demon, whoever you are, and I demand of you from this day, from this hour, from this moment, that ... be tormented on that day. I adjure you by him who released you from the bonds of life, O highest sea, air, and celestial god. Iao, ou, ia, iaaa, io, io-e, ooriuo, a, hia. Ocuria, anoch oton, barnion, formione, efecebul. Lynceus, let the fetlock be broken. I adjure you, demon, whoever you are, and I demand of you from this day, from this hour, from this moment, that ... be tormented. I adjure you by him who released you from the bonds of life, O highest sea, air, and celestial god. Iao, ou, ia, iaaa, io, io-e, ooriuo, a, hia. Lynceus.
EDCS-34100450.summary: This is a magical curse text, possibly a defixio, where the dedicator adjures a demon to torment individuals and break the fetlocks of horses, invoking powerful deities and divine names, and naming 'Lynceus' as a target or agent.

EDCS-34100451.translation: Ocuria, anoch oton, barnion, formione, efecebul. I adjure you, demon, whoever you are, and I demand that from this day, from this hour, from this moment, ... be tormented in the infernal abyss. I adjure you by him who released you from the bonds of life, O highest sea, air, and celestial god. Iao, ou, ia, iaaa, io, io-e, ooriuo, a, hia. Ocuria, anoch oton, barnion, formione, efecebul. Profugus, let Peciolus Frangrio be...
EDCS-34100451.summary: This is a magical curse text, likely a defixio, where the dedicator adjures a demon to torment individuals in the infernal abyss, invoking divine powers and specific names.

EDCS-34200064.summary: This is a fragmentary inscription that simply names Paulus Gentilis Saturninus.

EDCS-34200065.translation: To the sea-going Augustus, Aufidius Domitianus, Roman equestrian.
EDCS-34200065.summary: This is a dedication of a statue or monument to Emperor Augustus by a Roman knight, Aufidius Domitianus.

EDCS-34200066.translation: To Fulcinae Sabinae, from the public treasury of the municipality of Sufetula, of the Musunii family.
EDCS-34200066.summary: This is a dedication of a public work or monument to Fulcinae Sabinae by the municipality of Sufetula, funded by the Musunii family.

EDCS-34200067.summary: This is a funerary inscription for Victoria, dating from the Late Roman period.

EDCS-34200068.translation: In the most blessed and flourishing times of our lords Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, perpetual Augusti, while Manlius Crepereius Scipio Vincentius, a man of consular rank, administered the province of Flavia Valeria Byzacena, Titus Flavius Dyscolius Therapius, formerly a tribune, now a perpetual flamen and curator of the republic, out of civic love for his fatherland, improved and completed the square, which was an ornament to the city and to this natural location, by leveling the uneven, stony ground and enclosing it with columns and arches, thus making it more beautiful, and he happily dedicated it with an entertainment of games.
EDCS-34200068.summary: This is a dedication inscription for a public square in Flavia Valeria Byzacena, funded by Titus Flavius Dyscolius Therapius, likely dating to the late 4th or early 5th century AD.

EDCS-34200069.translation: Pray, holy ones, offering the gifts of God.
EDCS-34200069.summary: This is a religious inscription, possibly a votive offering or dedication, from the Late Roman period.

EDCS-34200073.translation: The tavern flourishes; drinking, it rejoices to protect its guest.
EDCS-34200073.summary: This is a short, epigrammatic inscription found on a tavern, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-34200074.translation: Dear nurse, may you always favor and increase the Canneani.
EDCS-34200074.summary: This is a dedicatory or commendatory inscription, possibly for a nurse or a person associated with the 'Canneani', from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-34200075.translation: Publius Iulius Sabinianus, a prudent man, most learned in all authors, a master of frugality, lived 34 years, 5 months, and 3 days.
EDCS-34200075.summary: This is a funerary inscription recording the life span of Publius Iulius Sabinianus, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-34200076.translation: April and September: hours 1 and 11, 24 feet; hours 2 and 10, 14 feet; hours 3 and 9, 10 feet; hours 4 and 8, 7 feet; hours 5 and 7, 5 feet; hour 6, only 4 feet. May and August: hours 1 and 11, 23 feet; hours 2 and 10, 13 feet; hours 3 and 9, 9 feet; hours 4 and 8, 6 feet; hours 5 and 7, 4 feet; hour 6, only 3 feet. June and July: hours 1 and 11, 22 feet; hours 2 and 10, 12 feet; hours 3 and 9, 8 feet; hours 4 and 8, 5 feet; hours 5 and 7, 3 feet; hour 6, only 2 feet. I made this by order of our lord father Iaquintus the bishop, in Carthage, in the district of the citadel, at Placidiana Fatia.
EDCS-34200076.summary: This inscription records shadow lengths measured at different hours for various months, commissioned by Bishop Iaquintus in Carthage, likely dating from the Late Roman or Early Byzantine period.

EDCS-34200078.translation: Baracho, son of Metthumbalis Addibalis, donated a column in the temple of Saturn; he took care to have it placed at his own expense.
EDCS-34200078.summary: This is a dedication inscription for a column in the temple of Saturn, funded by Baracho, son of Metthumbalis Addibalis, likely from Roman North Africa.

EDCS-34200080.text_edition: \n Imperatori Caesari Lucio Septimio Severo Pio Pertinaci Augusto Arabico Adiabenico Parthico maximo tribunicia potestate VII imperatori IX consuli II patri patriae Quintus Lollius Quinti filius Quirina Saturninus equo publico exornatus IIvir quinquennalis praeter alia in rem publicam et erga cives beneficia ob honorem quinquennalitatis inlatis rei publicae HS VI milibus sedem quoque domino nostro Severo Augusto designato ab ordine loco sua pecunia posuit idemque dedicavit\n
EDCS-34200080.translation: Quintus Lollius Saturninus, son of Quintus, of the Quirina tribe, honored with the equestrian order, quinquennial duovir, placed and dedicated this seat at his own expense, at his own location, for our lord Severus Augustus designated by the council, in addition to other benefits to the state and citizens, for the honor of his quinquennial term, with 6,000 sesterces contributed to the state, for Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pius Pertinax Augustus Arabicus Adiabenicus Parthicus Maximus, chief priest, with tribunician power for the 7th time, imperator for the 9th time, consul for the 2nd time, father of his country.
EDCS-34200080.summary: This inscription records Quintus Lollius Saturninus dedicating a seat in honor of Emperor Septimius Severus, funded by himself and with public contributions, during his term as quinquennial duovir.

EDCS-34200081.text_edition: \n Imperatori Caesari Marco Aurelio Antonino Augusto Pio principi iuventutis Imperatoris Caesaris Luci Septimi Severi Pii Pertinacis Augusti Arabici Adiabenici Parthici maximi filio divi Marci Antonini Pii Germanici Sarmatici nepoti divi Antonini Pii pronepoti divi Hadriani abnepoti divi Traiani Parthici et divi Nervae adnepoti praeterquam quod [] statuam togatam posuit item rei publicae summam duumviratus legitimam intulit Marcus Agrius Ulpius Primanus IIvir ex reliquiis et liberalitate pollicitus basem posuit\n
EDCS-34200081.translation: To the Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Pius, prince of the youth, son of Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pius Pertinax Augustus Arabicus Adiabenicus Parthicus Maximus, grandson of the deified Marcus Antoninus Pius Germanicus Sarmaticus, great-grandson of the deified Antoninus Pius, great-great-grandson of the deified Hadrian, great-great-great-grandson of the deified Trajan Parthicus and the deified Nerva. Marcus Agrius Ulpius Primanus, as twice-magistrate, who had promised a togate statue and also the full inheritance of the office of twice-magistrate to the state, erected the base from remaining funds and his own generosity.
EDCS-34200081.summary: This inscription records the erection of a statue base by Marcus Agrius Ulpius Primanus, a local magistrate, to honor Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (likely Caracalla) and fulfill a public vow, dating to his reign (c. 198-217 AD).

EDCS-34200082.text_edition: \n Imperatori Caesari Marco Aurelio Antonino Augusto Pio principi iuventutis Imperatoris Caesaris Luci Septimi Severi Pii Pertinacis Augusti Arabici Adiabenici Parthici maximi filio divi Marci Antonini Pii Germanici Sarmatici nepoti divi Antonini Pii pronepoti divi Hadriani abnepoti divi Traiani Parthici et divi Nervae adnepoti sedemL cum statua togata et filius eius Quintus Domitius Luci filius Quirina Pudens IIvir liberalitate pollicitus sua pecunia summam quoque honorariam IIviratus\n
EDCS-34200082.translation: To the Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Pius, prince of the youth, son of Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pius Pertinax Augustus Arabicus Adiabenicus Parthicus Maximus, grandson of the deified Marcus Antoninus Pius Germanicus Sarmaticus, great-grandson of the deified Antoninus Pius, great-great-grandson of the deified Hadrian, great-great-great-grandson of the deified Trajan Parthicus and the deified Nerva. Quintus Domitius Pudens, son of Lucius, of the Quirina tribe, twice-magistrate, who promised a seat with a togate statue and also the full honorarium for the office of twice-magistrate, erected it with his own money, as well as his son.
EDCS-34200082.summary: This inscription records the erection of a seat with a statue by Quintus Domitius Pudens and his son, local magistrates, to honor Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (likely Caracalla), funded by their own generosity, dating to his reign (c. 198-217 AD).

EDCS-34200083.text_edition: \n Ex auctoritate Imperatoris Nervae Traiani Caesaris Augusti Germanici Dacici consulis VI imperatoris XIIII Lucius Acilius Strabo Clodius Nummus legatus Augusti pro praetore inter Musulamios et Siccenses\n
EDCS-34200083.translation: By the authority of Emperor Nerva Trajan Caesar Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, Consul VI, Imperator XIIII. Lucius Acilius Strabo Clodius Nummus, imperial legate with praetorian power, between the Musulamii and the Siccenses.
EDCS-34200083.summary: This inscription records an administrative decision or boundary settlement made by the Roman legate Lucius Acilius Strabo Clodius Nummus, acting under the authority of Emperor Trajan, likely in North Africa, dating to Trajan's reign (98-117 AD).

EDCS-34500001.summary: This is a dedication inscription to the goddess Caelestis, likely from Roman North Africa.

EDCS-34500135.translation: Doliary work from the estates of our Augustus, Caius Cominius Sabinianus.
EDCS-34500135.summary: This inscription records pottery production from the estates of Caius Cominius Sabinianus, likely from Roman Italy.

EDCS-34600048.inscription_type: tituli honorarii, tituli operum, tituli sacri
EDCS-34600048.text_edition: \n Ex indulgentia domini nostri Imperatoris Caesaris divi Severi Pii nepotis divi Magni Antonini fili Marci Aureli Severi Alexandri Pii Felicis Augusti pontificis maximi tribunicia potestate VIIII consulis III patris patriae proconsulis colonia Alexandriana Augusta Uchi maius sub eius nomine auspicioque deducta per Caesonium Lucillum clarissimum virum partes proconsulis PONTM vices administrantem monumentum ad aeternum testimonium reciperatae libertatis erexit pecunia publica\n
EDCS-34600048.translation: By the indulgence of our lord Emperor Caesar, grandson of the deified Severus Pius, son of the deified Magnus Antoninus, Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander Pius Felix Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the 9th time, Consul III, Father of the Fatherland, Proconsul. The colony of Alexandria Augusta Uchi Maius, founded under his name and auspices, was established by Caesennius Lucillus, a most distinguished man, administering the duties of the proconsul, erected this monument at public expense as an eternal testimony to its recovered liberty.
EDCS-34600048.summary: This inscription records the foundation of the colony of Alexandria Augusta Uchi Maius under the auspices of Emperor Severus Alexander, with a monument erected by Caesennius Lucillus to commemorate the city's restored liberty, dating to Severus Alexander's reign (222-235 AD).

EDCS-34600054.translation: Gaius Numisius Quadratus, son of Us, a Roman knight, and his wife Utia Honorata Agriana, daughter of Munificus, who held the office of aedile and duovir twice, gave a banquet for the people and the local council of Uchita Maiora in honour of the fourth [consulship?].
EDCS-34600054.summary: This inscription records a dedication by Gaius Numisius Quadratus and his wife Utia Honorata Agriana, who provided a banquet for the town and its council.

EDCS-34600064.translation: Place of the god SVF VE, place of Janus, consul Felix, place of S M PR, for loans, forum of Alexi, Alexsi C SVF NI II IV.
EDCS-34600064.summary: This inscription appears to be a record of land ownership or a commercial notice related to a forum and financial transactions.

EDCS-34600096.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Sextus Aemilius Forsum, pious, lived [for X years]. He is buried here.

EDCS-34600119.summary: This is a funerary epitaph for Fortunatus, son of Sextus Octavius, who died at the age of 35.

EDCS-34600126.translation: Titus Suellius Vitalis, whom this colony received, here restored his last breath, two days short of sixteen years of age; a most wretched father set this up; here he lies. Abledo.
EDCS-34600126.summary: This funerary inscription records the death of Titus Suellius Vitalis at the age of 15 years and 363 days, set up by his grieving father.

EDCS-34600127.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Lucius Titurnius Felix, son of Lucius, of the Arnensis tribe, dutiful, lived 65 years; here he lies.
EDCS-34600127.summary: This funerary inscription records the life and burial of Lucius Titurnius Felix, who lived to be 65 years old.

EDCS-34600128.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Marcus Tullius Felix, dutiful, lived 55 years; here he lies.

EDCS-34600131.translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed. Vulceia Felicitas, dutiful, lived 25 years; here she lies.

EDCS-34600132.translation: Marcus Volteius Fortunatus, son of Marcus, of the Arnensis tribe, dutiful, lived 39 years; here he lies.

EDCS-34800167.translation: May 16. Total 59. Of these: 1 scribe, 1 optio, 21 quintanarii, 3 stationarii, 5 for the bath water, 1 for the straps, 1 for Boinag(?), 7 sick. The rest are working. 19 [personnel]. [Bath]house. Sick: Aurelius Carinas, Julius [---]
EDCS-34800167.summary: This inscription appears to be a daily report or roster, possibly for a military unit or public works crew, detailing personnel assigned to various duties including bath maintenance and listing sick individuals, dated to May 16th, likely from the 3rd century AD.

EDCS-34800170.translation: June 16. Total 86. Recruits: 64. Of these: 3 equites, 22 quintanarii, 8 for the bathhouse, 1 from the cistern, 1 for the overseer, 1 for the camelry station, 1 optio. Also Rufus: 2 sick. 28 are excused. The remaining 26 are diligent. The bathhouse receives.
EDCS-34800170.summary: This inscription is a daily report detailing the numbers and assignments of recruits and other personnel, including those assigned to the bathhouse and excused duties, dating to June 16th, likely from the 3rd century AD.

EDCS-34800173.translation: August 1. Total 44. Of these: 1 scribe, 1 optio, 1 proculcator, 7 for the bath water, 5 stationarii, 1 miller, 1 furnace worker, 1 for the prison. Sick: Paccius Maximus, 1 with 3 camels. The remaining 22 are working. The bathhouse receives 16 [personnel] and 1 camel driver. The furnace receives 5.
EDCS-34800173.summary: This inscription is a daily report listing personnel assigned to various duties, including bath operations, a mill, a furnace, and a prison, along with sick individuals and those managing camels, dated to August 1st, likely from the 3rd century AD.

EDCS-34800177.translation: September 21. Total 58. Of these: 9 equites, 1 optio, 14 quintanarii, 6 for the bath water, 1 from the cistern, 1 for the overseer, 1 sent to Esuba, 1 craftsman. 3 sick: Julius Ianuarius, Julius the sesquiplicarius, Caecilius Rogatus. The remaining 21 are working. The bathhouse receives 16. The furnace receives 5.
EDCS-34800177.summary: This inscription is a daily report detailing personnel, including cavalrymen and specialists, assigned to various tasks and listing three sick individuals, with numbers for bathhouse and furnace staff, dated to September 21st, likely from the 3rd century AD.

EDCS-34800182.translation: November 11. Total 45. Of these: 1 sesquiplicarius Aurelius Celestinus, [3] equites Caecilius Rogatus, 1 optio Aurelius Quirinus, [3] quintanarii, 2 for the bathhouse, [3] from the cisterns. [---]
EDCS-34800182.summary: This inscription is a partial daily report listing personnel, including a sesquiplicarius, equites, and an optio, along with numbers for bathhouse and cistern assignments, dated to November 11th, likely from the 3rd century AD.

EDCS-34800189.translation: [---] Total 44 [personnel]. Of these: 1 scribe, 1 optio, 1 proculcator [---], 3 for the bathhouse, 13 quintanarii, 4 stationarii. 2 sick. Paccius Maximus, Julius Secundarius: 2 [individuals]. The rest are working, a total of 19. The bathhouse receives 12, the furnace worker 7.
EDCS-34800189.summary: This inscription is a fragmented daily report detailing personnel assignments, including scribes, optiones, and quintanarii, with numbers for bathhouse and furnace staff, and listing sick individuals, likely from the 3rd century AD.

EDCS-34800190.translation: XV quintanarii (soldiers serving for a 5-year term?), 6 to the bath water, III stationarii (stationed soldiers?), 1 to Esuba, 1 to the treasury, 2 sick. Pacius Maximus, Pompeus Datius. The rest await(?), XV. Bath 3, furnace.
EDCS-34800190.summary: This inscription is a list of personnel and their assignments, possibly related to military or administrative duties, including mentions of baths and a furnace, dated to the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-34800192.translation: II stationarii, 1 sent with the Garamantes, 1 guard, 3 or 4 sick. Farbius [3]s [[Aurel 3]]. Aurelius Felix, Julius Priscus, Julius Optatus. The rest await(?), XXIIII.
EDCS-34800192.summary: This inscription appears to be a roll call or roster listing soldiers and their statuses, including an engagement with the Garamantes and mentioning sick personnel, likely from the Roman military.

EDCS-34800194.translation: 1 to the prefect, 1 craftsman, 2 sick. Aurelius Celestinus, Cecil(ius) Rogatus. The rest await(?), XVI. The bath receives [3]. Furnace.

EDCS-34800195.translation: 1 sick. Cecil(ius) Rogatus. The rest await(?), XVI. The bath receives XII. Furnace IIII.

EDCS-34800196.translation: 1 optio (officer), XV quintanarii, 6 to the bath water, 1 from the watch posts, 1 to the standards, 1 to the prefect, 1 to the rods (punishment?), 2 sick. Cornelius Hannibal, Aurelius Celestinus. The rest await(?).

EDCS-34800197.translation: III sick. Cornelius Hannibal, Aurelius Celestinus, Caecilius Rogatus. The rest await(?), XVIII. Bath XIIII, furnace IIII.

EDCS-34800198.translation: 1 to the prefect, 1 to the bath. III sick. Cornelius Hannibal, Aurelius Celestinus, Caecilius Rogatus. The rest await(?), XVIII. The bath receives(?) VII. Furnace VI.

EDCS-34800240.translation: To Octavius Festus, my decurion and prefect, Aemilius Aemilianus, soldier, greetings. EDCS-34900999.text_edition: \n Imperatore Domitiano Caesare Augusto Germanico XIIII consule iuventus civitatis Mactaritanae cultores Martis Augusti solo publico basilicam et horrea II pecunia sua faciendum curaverunt curatoribus Saturnino Arisim filio et Fortunato Lulhim filio magistri Saturninus Leptha filius Aris Chunin filius Rogatus Addunis filius Fortunatus Arsaces filius Silvanus Mutthumbalis filius Balsillec Zrumae filius Nanes Thusabiae filius Baricbal Iasuctani filius Primus Victoris filius Gudul Mazbalis filius Saturninus Fortunati filius Cittin Selidiunis filius Ninus Iassicbalis filius Baric Sappir filius Mitthun Samonis filius Aris Arisim filius Fortunatus Papi filius Sfichinnius Mercatoris filius Optatus Laeti filius Mitthun Mutthumbalis filius Baliathon ilian filius Victor Balsamonis filius Felix Fortis filius Aris Zruman filius Mustu Musthumbalis filius Rogatus Fausti filius Bassus Maximi filius Faustus Sexti filius Ninus Baricbalis filius Mitthumbal Rogati filius Crescens Baricis libertus Titus Iaraucan filius Gudul Thilbran filius Birzic Maximi filius Maximus Optati filius Rogatus ri filius Publius Fortis filius Ialival Bassi filius Maximus Iurathai filius Mustu Zrumai filius Macarsa Quinti filius Fortunatus A--- f(ilius) Rogatus Tertullae filius Rogatus Largi Africanus Ardeumai filius Satur Birissio filius Datus Thiai filius Rogatus Faustae filius Messor Tertullae filius Satur Aris filius NovMuthumbalis filius Baricbal Fidae filius Ninus Adarbalis filius Aris Cantoris filius Vassai Rogatae filius Fortunatus Oricionis filius Sfichenius Mitthunis Vindex Bassi Birzic Zrumai filius Ciri Bassi filius Martialis Acchana filius Lucrio Sexti filius Martialis Fav filius Cinsais filius Cai Chachonis filius Saturninus Zrumanis Baliathon Tafibra\n
EDCS-34900999.translation: During the consulship of Emperor Domitian Caesar Augustus Germanicus for the 14th time, the youth of the Mactaritan community, worshippers of Mars Augustus, built this public basilica and two storehouses with their own money. They were supervised by curators Saturninus, son of Arisim, and Fortunatus, son of Lulh(im), and under the magistracy of Saturninus, son of Leptha, and other community leaders and patrons, including Aris son of Chunin, Rogatus son of Addunis, Fortunatus son of Arsaces, Silvanus son of Mutthumbalis, Balsillec son of Zrumae, Nanes son of Thusabiae, Baricbal son of Iasuctani, Primus son of Victor, Gudul son of Mazbalis, Saturninus son of Fortunati, Cittin son of Selidiunis, Ninus son of Iassicbalis, Baric son of Sappir, Mitthun son of Samonis, Aris son of Arisim, Fortunatus son of Papi, Sfichinnius son of Mercatoris, Optatus son of Laeti, Mitthun son of Mutthumbalis, Baliathon son of Ilian, Victor son of Balsamonis, Felix son of Fortis, Aris son of Zruman, Mustu son of Musthumbalis, Rogatus son of Fausti, Bassus son of Maximi, Faustus son of Sexti, Ninus son of Baricbalis, Mitthum son of Rogati, Crescens freedman of Baricis, Titus son of Iaraucan, Gudul son of Thilbran, Birzic son of Maximi, Maximus son of Optati, Rogatus son of Ri, Publius son of Fortis, Ialival son of Bassi, Maximus son of Iurathai, Mustu son of Zrumai, Macarsa son of Quinti, Fortunatus son of A---, Rogatus son of Tertulla, Rogatus son of Largi Africanus, Ardeumai son of Satur, Birissio son of Datus, Thiai son of Rogatus, Faustae son of Messor, Tertullae son of Satur, Aris son of Nov, Muthumbalis son of Baricbal, Fidae son of Ninus, Adarbalis son of Aris, Cantoris son of Vassai, Rogatae son of Fortunatus, Oricionis son of Sfichenius, Mitthunis Vindex son of Bassi, Birzic son of Zrumai, Ciri son of Bassi, Martialis son of Acchana, Lucrio son of Sexti, Martialis son of Fav, Cinsais son of Cai, Chachonis son of Saturninus, Zrumanis, Baliathon son of Tafibra.
EDCS-34900999.summary: This inscription records the construction of a public basilica and storehouses by the youth of Mactaritan, dedicated to Mars Augustus, during the consulship of Domitian and lists numerous community leaders and patrons who contributed or were involved.

EDCS-35001070.translation: 13 days before the Kalends of June, a total of 3 [individuals/units?]; among them: 1 sesquiplicarius, 6 equites, 1 optio, 10 quintanarii, 2 for the water of the bathhouse, 2 for the camels, 1 for the prefect, 1 craftsman, 1 sick person. Caecilius Rogatus... the rest shall pay back... 8 bathhouse attendants, 5 furnace workers.
EDCS-35001070.summary: This is a fragmented list of personnel and their duties or numbers, likely related to the administration of a bathhouse or similar facility, with a date indicated as 13 days before the Kalends of June.

EDCS-36100345.translation: Pottery production from the estates of Lucilla, under the consulship of Verus Severus and Sabinianus.
EDCS-36100345.summary: A document recording pottery production from the estates of Lucilla, dated by the consuls Verus Severus and Sabinianus.

EDCS-36100346.summary: An inscription indicating ownership or a dedication by Gnaeus Domitius Evaristus, likely related to property or a building.

EDCS-36100349.translation: From the estates of Flavius Aper, pottery production by Lars.
EDCS-36100349.summary: An inscription detailing pottery production from the estates of Flavius Aper, attributed to Lars.

EDCS-36100350.translation: From the workshops of Marcus Herennius Pollio, pottery of Lucius Sestius Successus.
EDCS-36100350.summary: An inscription indicating pottery production, specifying the workshop of Marcus Herennius Pollio and the producer Lucius Sestius Successus.

EDCS-36400004.text_edition: \n Hic Vibius Felix si tempora longa fuissent Felix epulis cognomine fortem neverim nam septem simul et viginti viximus annos nunc quoniam Parcae rumpunt breve fila sorores patris mente pia pariter karaque sepultus hoc situs in tumulo felix in mortem quiesco\n
EDCS-36400004.translation: If times had been long, I, Vibius Felix, would have wished to say that Felix, strong in his surname, had lived seven and twenty years together. But now, since the Fates break the short threads of sisters, buried by my father’s pious mind and also dear, I lie in this tomb, happy in death, I rest.
EDCS-36400004.summary: This is an epitaph for Vibius Felix, composed in elegiac couplets, lamenting his short life of twenty-seven years and expressing his contentment in death.

EDCS-36400005.text_edition: \n Hic sita est Kasta Magni rarissima coniunx quae vixit semper parce et sine fraude beata pro dolore pia est misera brevi tempore fati sancta pudicitia vixit denis quater annis o dulcis coniunx uita mihi dulcior ipsa concordes linquens generum tuumque maritum hanc aram Magnus posuit karissimae Kastae\n
EDCS-36400005.translation: Here lies Kasta Magna, his rarest wife, who lived always with restraint and without deceit, blessed. In her grief, pious, miserable, she lived a short time in fate, chaste, modest. She lived thirty-six years. Oh sweet wife, sweeter to me than life itself, leaving concord, your son-in-law and your husband, Magnus erected this altar for his dearest Kasta.
EDCS-36400005.summary: This is a funerary altar erected by Magnus for his wife Kasta, who lived a virtuous life and died at the age of 36.

EDCS-36400006.text_edition: \n ius Luci filius Arnensi Fortunatus vixit annis IV hic situs est RN teneris sic puer iacet sub pondere magno annis uixi IV dulcissumus sic parentibus in V annum ascendens hic animam posui cui puero mater mama posuisse viderus sic huic puero lapidem supremum redidit ipsa\n
EDCS-36400006.translation: Lucius, son of Lucius, of the Arnensian tribe, Fortunatus, lived 4 years. Here he lies. Tender boy, he lies under a great weight. I lived 4 years, most sweet. Ascending into the fifth year, I surrendered my soul here. To whom, mother, it seemed, Mama placed this stone, the last one for this boy, she herself gave it.
EDCS-36400006.summary: This is a tombstone for a young boy named Fortunatus, who died at the age of 4 and was buried by his mother Mama.

EDCS-36400007.text_edition: \n F O N e a vitae tantem lus atque mo satyros perfedentis dulcia orum frequentora movit et quiq qui suas fabulas in tempore finxit easdem meditans semper elusit n se placuit ut voluit puer molliora fratri \n
EDCS-36400007.translation: An example of life, so much joy and satyrs, pleasing sweet things, and he who in his time finished his stories, always meditating on the same ones, he amused himself. He pleased himself as he wished, softer than his brother.
EDCS-36400007.summary: This fragmentary inscription seems to praise a person's life, possibly an actor or poet, known for their joyful performances and stories.

EDCS-36400008.text_edition: \n Hic sita sedibus tot tollens o Claudia co o utinam t R frui d SAV\n
EDCS-36400008.translation: Here lies, raised to the seats of the gods, oh Claudia, oh R... may you enjoy...
EDCS-36400008.summary: This is a very fragmentary epitaph for a Claudia, likely indicating her burial or transition to the divine.

EDCS-36400009.translation: Accept, dear parent, the sweet praises of life, which you often in your years led Asellus to pleasures for Venus, you were not sparing of Bacchus's vessel, so that you leave nothing to companions.
EDCS-36400009.summary: A poem inscribed on a monument, likely a tomb, praising a deceased parent's joyful and generous life, particularly their enjoyment of wine and companionship.

EDCS-36400010.text_edition: \n VIIDA vixit annos LX Fortunatus filius posuit quid simus aut quid loquimur vitast id denique nostra cum reputem VM LE quoque dispicio vel modo SIS cum vixit homo nunc homo NEST est hominis praeter cana favilla L stat LANS et nomen tantum vestigiu N est inscriptu est hominis cetera memNI CVRTEA N VIS Crusias denique AV uerunt non sunt NOS quoque mus vivit et dum quest aetas dum VNDA voluptas non est aeternum\n
EDCS-36400010.translation: VIIDA lived 60 years. Fortunatus, his son, placed this. What we are, or what we say, life is just that. When I consider it, I see that when a man lived, now he is not a man. Nothing remains of man but white ash. L stands, and only the name, a trace of man is inscribed, the rest is memory. CVRTEA N VIS Crusias finally... they lived, we too... life is as long as pleasure lasts, it is not eternal.
EDCS-36400010.summary: This epitaph reflects on the ephemeral nature of life, stating that only a name and ashes remain after death, likely for a man named Fortunatus who lived to 60.

EDCS-36400011.text_edition: \n tas hominum mos est bene vivere et post obitum nomen habere cara pia coniux Vaninna cum Valio Victorico sancto marito periit V LVM NOSA\n
EDCS-36400011.translation: It is the custom of men's lives to live well and to have a name after death. My dear, pious wife Vaninna perished with her holy husband Valio Victoricus. V LVM NOSA
EDCS-36400011.summary: This epitaph states that it is customary for people to live well and be remembered after death, and records the passing of Vaninna with her husband Valio Victoricus.

EDCS-36400013.translation: Sacred to the departed spirits. I was content with all things. Preserving this with affectionate, bright eyes, not [as property] to the gods but if such a heart is more honorable, chaste, and lustful, I am not [in this world].
EDCS-36400013.summary: A philosophical or devotional funerary inscription dedicated to the 'Dis Manibus', reflecting on contentment, virtue, and the nature of the soul after death.

EDCS-36400014.text_edition: \n ICR Acherusiae tenebrae et Elysii coluntur quinquaginta licet septem annos sex menses atque simum et decem dies eri quos tribuerit relicta vita cessit hic situs est\n
EDCS-36400014.translation: The darkness of Acheron and the Elysian Fields are honored. He lived fifty-seven years, six months, and ten days, then he departed from life. Here he lies.
EDCS-36400014.summary: This epitaph records the death of an individual who lived 57 years, 6 months, and 10 days, and mentions the realms of the afterlife.

EDCS-36400015.text_edition: \n Aquiliae Quinti filiae Flaccillae c(larissimae)? f(eminae) Quintus Silius Luci filius Arnensi Maurus amicus ob merita quod beneficio liberalitate eius paternis necessitatibus exsolutus dignitatis suae conservatus est decreto decurionum\n
EDCS-36400015.translation: To Aquilia Flaccilla, daughter of Quintus, a most distinguished woman. Quintus Silius Maurus, son of Lucius, of the Arnensian tribe, as a friend, because he was freed from his paternal necessities by her merit and generosity and was preserved in his dignity, by decree of the decurions.
EDCS-36400015.summary: This inscription honors Aquilia Flaccilla, a distinguished woman, and records the gratitude of Quintus Silius Maurus, who was aided by her generosity, as recognized by a decree of the decurions.

EDCS-38600001.translation: Kill, exterminate, wound Gallicus, whom Prima bore, at this hour in the amphitheater's circle, and for the games I prepare this… Binding his hands, blindfold him. It is not permissible for the bear, the bears… binding his feet, his limbs, his senses, his marrow. Binding Gallicus, whom Prima bore, so that he may not kill the bear or the bull with single blows, nor with double blows, nor with triple blows. The bull, the bear, by the name of the living, all-powerful God, may you complete it! Now, now, quickly, quickly, let the bear strike him and wound him!
EDCS-38600001.summary: This is a magical text, likely a curse or incantation, intended to ensure the survival of a gladiator named Gallicus in a combat against a bear and a bull during games, possibly dating to the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700204.summary: This is a very short inscription that appears to be an owner's mark or dedication, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700263.translation: Valerius EpaphrHoditus, Valerius Oncarpus, Valerius Pleogius, Valerius Onomacus, Valerius Sabinus, Valerius Herma, Valerius Maternus, Valerius Romanus, Valerius Trophimus, Plotius Hermes, Critonius Faustus, Valerius Hermes, Valeria Omphale, Valeria Trophine, Valeria Flora, va
EDCS-38700263.summary: This inscription lists numerous personal names, likely belonging to a group of freedmen and freedwomen or a family, possibly associated with a funerary monument from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700264.translation: Scribonia Philomusus, Crison, Alypus, Lerastus, Philargurus, Avner, Felix, Liberalis, my fellow freedmen and freedwomen, friends, family members, relatives, and whomever else who has tried, spoken, acted, or wished to act, fellow freedmen or freedwomen.
EDCS-38700264.summary: This text appears to be a legal or ritualistic declaration, likely related to a funerary context, outlining individuals who are associated with the deceased and invoking a curse on anyone who acts against them, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700265.translation: may my fisci tongue not be able to speak or act against me, except what I wish. I bind and select the tongues of the obstinate, of the clever, of the wise, of the skillful. By the nets of Primus, and by the trireme and by the motive of my parents, and by the necessity of my parents, and by my father's victory, may they not be angry against me. I bind that tongue and… of Pudentis, I bind and select the tongue of… Calligraphae.
EDCS-38700265.summary: This is a magical inscription, likely a curse intended to silence enemies or adversaries, invoking divine and familial powers, probably from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700266.translation: Of Sextilianus and Gula Pudentis, and of Pacorus Acutus and Marcus, son of Silvanus, and of Sextilianus, and of Lucius Caecilius Magnus. Bind the tongues of these whom I have written above, so that they may not respond against us. Arasbetharabespygoe phintibor.
EDCS-38700266.summary: This inscription is a curse intended to silence specific individuals, likely enemies or adversaries, invoking divine powers and possibly including Greek or foreign magical words, possibly from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700267.translation: I indicate him, and may you make them mute in opposition to Atlosa. I bind and obligate the tongues of those people, the middle, the ends, the last, so that they can do nothing in response against. Make them mute, mutos, gallos, mutulos, Crispum, by the sea and Marine, by parinis, I obligate the tongues of those people, their sockets, their limbs, their heart, ...
EDCS-38700267.summary: This inscription is a magical curse aimed at rendering specific individuals mute and powerless against someone named Atlosa, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700268.translation: Lady Terra, make Germanus mute. Accommodate. I implore you, guardians of Opsecra Isperata, and Martialus, Cosconius, Ianuarius, and Rufus, to make those who are there mute and full of fear, whose names you have here, so that they cannot speak against Opsecra Isperata, so that enemies cannot speak against her.
EDCS-38700268.summary: This is a magical invocation to the earth goddess and other deities to silence and instill fear in the enemies of Opsecra Isperata, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700269.translation: Securus, how can he not speak against us? Thus they may not speak against my father, against me, the advocates who cannot argue with him, as if our rights were a rug. Toresilius, and whoever comes, just as letters cannot be to anyone, so no one can come to him. Just as Securus cannot speak, so advocates who, whoever, cannot speak.
EDCS-38700269.summary: This inscription is a complex magical text or curse, using rhetorical questions and comparisons to ensure silence and prevent legal or verbal opposition against the author and their father, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700270.translation: Claudia Helenis, Clodia Successa, Clodia Steretia, Clodius Fortunatus, Clodius Romanus, Murcius Crimenius, Servilius Faustus, Valerius Extricatus. Just as I have given these names to the underworld, so may all be mute against me, so that they cannot speak. Just as I have torn out and fixed the tongue of this rooster alive, so may the tongues of my enemies be mute against me. Thus may he who has dared to speak against me be reduced to nothing. This plea is guaranteed. I implore you, mute ones, through your victory, O Manes, thus may you place, and thus against.
EDCS-38700270.summary: This is a powerful magical curse, employing imagery of silencing enemies, sacrificing a rooster, and invoking the underworld spirits (Manes) to ensure absolute muteness and destruction for adversaries, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-38700272.translation: I care for you and have left you and now I approach Oppius... [---] on behalf of my enemies, Ulpia Publica, with her hostile tongue, and you, and whoever else has a tongue, tongues, tongues of tongues, may Flaccus Rufus be punished for this... [---] not to be able to do
EDCS-38700272.summary: This inscription appears to be a curse or a spell, possibly related to legal disputes or personal animosity, mentioning enemies and invoking curses.

EDCS-38700275.translation: May you cause them to perish, cause them to perish; may the speaking demon quickly lead me to oblivion; come, come, cause it from this day, from this hour; come, come, cause it until she returns; until she returns; come, come, cause it.
EDCS-38700275.summary: This text is a magical spell, likely a curse or binding, invoking a demon to cause oblivion and bring someone back.

EDCS-38700276.translation: You who are the great daemon of Egypt, take away sleep from him until he comes to me and satisfies my soul. Trabaxian, omnipotent daemon, bring a lover burning with my love and desire. Noxthirif, who compels, daemon, compel her to have intercourse with me. Bibirixi, who are the strongest daemon, urge and compel her to come to me, a lover burning with my love and desire. Rikourith, most agile daemon in Egypt, stir her from her parents, from her bedchamber and surroundings, whoever she holds dear, and compel her to love me, to bring herself to me for my desire. Kyrie, or whatever god or goddess you are, make her do [---]
EDCS-38700276.summary: This is a complex love-binding spell invoking multiple daemons to compel a specific person to love the petitioner and come to them.

EDCS-38700277.translation: I announce that the soul of the king is detained by her. So may your soul be detained forever in love and desire for Martialicus, whom Coronaria gave birth to. I adjure you, by this prefect over the needs of the earth, and by the Lord of the earth, that from this day, this moment, she may love Martialicus, so that in every feminine hour she may have me in her mind, and the whole day have my love in her mind. Oh great one, you lord, now, now.
EDCS-38700277.summary: This inscription is a powerful love spell invoking spirits and a lord to bind a woman named Coronaria to love Martialicus.

EDCS-38700278.translation: Bylamo... I invoke you, great and powerful, holding and dominating and binding with unbreakable, eternal, strong, adamantine chains. [---] restrain and bind the soul of [---] and subdue, subjugate, incline Sapaoutoulos. Bind him, seal him, so that he does not leave this place, nor the gate, nor depart from the place, but remains bound in your strong, eternal, adamantine chains, the soul of Sapaoutoulos, for Ponponia. [---] Let him be bound, obligated, let his feet not carry him, let his nerves not carry him against the earth, let him not be able to move. Let Sapaoutoulos's feet be bound, so he cannot run. Let him be obligated, let his feet and nerves [---] so that he does not possess [---] him. I make Sapaoutoulos do all things. His January in every moment. Now quickly. Bylamo... he who is bound...
EDCS-38700278.summary: This is a complex binding spell, likely from a magical papyrus, intended to immobilize and subjugate a person named Sapaoutoulos, ensuring they remain under the control of the petitioner for Ponponia.

EDCS-38700283.translation: Erekisiphthe... I invoke you, great and powerful, holding and dominating and binding with unbreakable, eternal, strong, adamantine chains. [---] Restrain and bind the soul of Sapaoutoulos, whoever he is, and subjugate him, incline him, bind him, seal him, so that he does not leave this place, nor the gate, nor depart from the place, but remains bound in your strong, eternal, adamantine chains, the soul of Sapaoutoulos, for Ponponia. [---] Let him be bound, obligated, let his feet not carry him, let his nerves not carry him against the earth, let him not be able to move. Let Sapaoutoulos's feet be bound, so he cannot run. Let him be obligated, let his feet and nerves [---] so that he does not possess [---] him. I make Sapaoutoulos do all things. His January in every moment. Now quickly. Bylamo... erekisiphthe...
EDCS-38700283.summary: This inscription is a magical spell, likely a binding or curse, similar to EDCS-38700278, invoking deities or powers to immobilize and control a person named Sapaoutoulos for the benefit of Ponponia.

EDCS-38700286.translation: I collect the middle, extreme, and latest tongues, so that you may not cause them to respond in vain. I collect the latest tongues, so that you may not cause them to respond. I make them mute with their tongues. I collect so that their help may not respond. I collect the middle, extreme, and latest tongues. I collect the middle, extreme, and latest tongues, so that they may not be able to do anything vain to me. I collect the middle, extreme, and latest tongues, so that you may not cause them to respond. I make them superior. I collect the middle, extreme, and latest tongues, so that you may not cause them to respond. I make them mute, mute. Publius Curtius, I collect, I bind them. I collect the middle, extreme, and latest tongues, so that you may not... I collect the tongues of the vain. I collect the middle, extreme, tongues, n [---]
EDCS-38700286.summary: This text appears to be a magical spell designed to disable or silence opponents, collecting their 'tongues' and preventing them from responding or acting.

EDCS-38700287.translation: Laelianus Saturninus, whom Aquilia Saturnina bore.
EDCS-38700287.summary: This is a simple parentage notice, recording the names of a father (Laelianus Saturninus) and his mother (Aquilia Saturnina).

EDCS-38700288.translation: Xalakh soumimarei... Victoria, whom her own vulva bore, the delight of girls.
EDCS-38700288.summary: This text is a magical invocation, possibly a love spell or charm, invoking divine names and describing 'Victoria' in a sensual and possibly ritualistic context.

EDCS-38700289.translation: Cogite Bonosam quam peperit Papte amare me Oppium quem peperit Veneria amore sacro sine intermissione non possit dormire Bonosa ne que esse Bonosa ne que aliud sed abrumpatur et me solum videret omnibus diebus adx us que ad diem mortis suae i. Cogite Bonosam quam peperit Papte amare me Oppium quem peperit Veneria amore sacro sine intermissione non possit dormire Bonosa ne que esse Bonosa ne que aliud sed abrumpatur et me solum videret omnibus diebus adx us que ad diem mortis suae i.
EDCS-38700289.summary: This is a love spell, likely from a magical papyrus, invoking powers to compel Bonosa, born of Papte, to love Oppius, born of Veneria, and to desire only him until death.

EDCS-38700290.translation: Persephone, obligated by me through Tialu, receive her in sense and wisdom and understanding and will, that which I demand from Bonosa, whom Bonosa bore, from this day, from this hour, to me, that she may forget father and mother. By my living god, heaven and earth, god, if he is under this crown, Arissore, I bind this noble woman. May she not be tormented by the earth and Semesilla, who is mine. Receive her, whom I commend to you, Bonosa, whom I commend to you, the priestess.
EDCS-38700290.summary: This is a curse inscription, likely from the Roman period in North Africa, where someone is cursing a woman named Bonosa to forget her parents and be tormented by unrequited love, invoking deities and cosmic forces.

EDCS-38700291.translation: This is the voice of the god. Who hears, hears. You, who are in the assembly, hear. Hear, you who are married. Hear, hear. O Lord, O Lord, pity! You are my master, my master. You are my master, you are my master. A vow of faith. You are my master. He who hears, hears. A vow of faith. He who hears, hears. He who hears, hears. He who hears, hears. He who hears, hears. He who hears, hears. He who hears, hears. In the holy place, in the sacred place. Come, you who are in the assembly, O Columbos. You will be in the place of the gods. You will be in the place of the gods. Come, you who are in the place of the gods. I have made it. Tottina, hear me. As long as you live, may you always think of me. Tottina, whom I bore, whom I bore. May you love me with your soul. My mistress has made it with love.
EDCS-38700291.summary: This text, written in a mixture of Latin and Greek with likely indigenous language elements, is a magical invocation or curse, possibly related to love or binding, dedicated to a deity or deities.

EDCS-38700292.translation: I adjure you by the great god and by Antherotas and by him who has the hawk above his head and by the seven stars that from this hour this will be composed: Sextillius, son of Dionisia, shall not sleep, shall burn, shall be mad, shall not sleep, nor shall he sit, nor shall he speak, but shall have in mind me, Septimia, daughter of Amoena. He shall burn, be mad, with my love and desire, his soul and heart shall burn. Sextillius, son of Dionisia, with my love and desire, the daughter of Septimia, daughter of Amoena. But you, Abar, Barbarie, Eloee, Sabaoth, Pachnoufu, Pythiepemi, make Sextillius, son of Dionisia, not touch sleep, but burn with my love and desire. His spirit and heart shall be consumed, all the members of his whole body. Sextillius, son of Dionisia, if I do not descend into the adyta of Osiris and dissolve... and send it by the river. For I am the great Decanus of the great god, the god AXRAMMAXALALAE.
EDCS-38700292.summary: This is a powerful love-binding curse inscription, likely from the Roman period, in Latin and Greek, where Septimia Amoena attempts to force Sextillius Dionisiae to be consumed by love for her, invoking multiple deities and magical formulae, and threatening dire consequences if her will is not met.

EDCS-38700298.summary: This inscription appears to be a personal name or a short epitaph, possibly referring to individuals named Margarita and Lynceus, with an uncertain context.

EDCS-38700338.translation: Pottery work from the Caninian workshops from the estates of Domitia Lucilla.
EDCS-38700338.summary: This is a maker's or ownership mark on a pottery item, indicating its origin from specific workshops and estates during the Roman period.

EDCS-39000028.translation: Here lies Larcis, who paid the price of life, seeing no light; I do not prefer death, but the dwelling of Ploutos and a bronze sleep, which all men desired. Alexandris bore me in Crete, known for its fruitfulness, for the sake of good sense and faithfulness. I lived 75 years in all wisdom and the clear path of life and usefulness. All these things were done by my devoted servants who treated me well, who raised my tomb, so that I might be known to all my friends and, though covered by death, speak among the living. Be of good cheer, Jesus Christ. No one is immortal.
EDCS-39000028.summary: This is an epitaph for Larcis, who lived 75 years and was known for wisdom and usefulness, set up by his devoted servants, likely from the Roman Imperial period given the Greek text and mention of 'Jesus Christ'.

EDCS-39000031.translation: Monument of Theudutas, daughter of Aiglanoros, son of Teimokrates. She died.

EDCS-39000176.translation: Semesilam, damatamenueus, lesthna, allam, laikam, ermoubele, iakoubiai, werbeth, iopakerbeth, homalthebeth, allasan. I adjure you by the great names that you bind every limb and every sinew of Victoricus, whom Mother Earth bore, the charioteer of the chariot and his horses, which Sekundinus is about to drive: Iubennus, and Atbokatos, and Boubalos, and Victoricus Pompeianus, and Vaianus, and Victor, and Eximius, and among the Messalians Dominator, and whoever else shall be yoked with them. Bind their legs, their charge, their leap, and their race. Blind their eyes, so they do not see. Twist their soul and their heart, so they do not breathe. Just as this rooster is bound in its feet, hands, and head, so bind the legs, hands, head, and heart of Victoricus, the charioteer of the chariot, on the coming day. And the horses which Sekundinus is about to drive: Iubennus, and Atbokatos, and Boubalos, and Laurianos, and Victoricus Pompeianus, and Vaianus, and Victor, and Eximius, and among the Messalians Dominator, and whoever else shall be yoked with them. Again I adjure you by the God above the heaven, who sits upon the Cherubim, who set the boundary of the earth and separated the sea, Iao, Abriao, Arbathiao, Sabaoth, Adonai, that you bind Victoricus, the charioteer of the chariot, and the horses which Sekundinus is about to drive: Iubennus, and Atouokatos, and Victoricus Pompeianus, and Vaianus, and Victor, and Eximius, and among the Messalians Dominator, that they may not come to victory on the coming day in the circus. Now, now, quickly, quickly!
EDCS-39000176.summary: This is a curse tablet, likely from the Roman Imperial period, intended to magically disable a charioteer named Victoricus and his horses in a chariot race, invoking powerful divine names.

EDCS-39100001.translation: I bind the spirit of the daemon dwelling here, by the holy name of Aoth Abraoth, the God of Abraham, and of Iao, the God of Jacob. Iao Aoth Abraoth, God of Israel, hear the venerable, fearful, and great name. And bring to her [or 'him'] to Orbanos, whom Urbana bore, Domitian, whom Candidus bore, loving, frenzied, sleepless for her love and desire, begging her to return to his house and become his wife. I adjure you by the great, eternal, and everlasting, and almighty God, who is above all gods, who created the heaven and the sea, who separated the righteous, who struck the rod in the sea, to bring and yoke Orbanos, whom Urbana bore, to Domitiana, whom Candidus bore, loving, tormented, sleepless for her desire and love, that he may lead her to his house as his wife. I adjure you, who made the mule not to breed. I adjure you, who set the boundary between light and darkness. I adjure you, who crushes rocks. I adjure you, who tears down mountains. I adjure you, who shakes the earth on its foundations. I adjure you by the holy name, which is not spoken, so that the demons may rise up astonished and terrified. Bring and yoke as a wife Orbanos, whom Urbana bore, to Domitiana, whom Candidus bore, loving and begging her, now, quickly. I adjure you by the maker of the luminaries and stars in the sky, by command, so that they shine for all men. I adjure you, who shook all the inhabited world and made mountains jut out and spew forth, who makes the whole earth tremble and renews all its inhabitants. I adjure you, who made signs in the sky, on earth, and in the sea, to bring and yoke as a wife Orbanos, whom Urbana bore, to Domitiana, whom Candidus bore, loving her and sleepless for her desire, begging her and asking her to return to his house and become his wife. I adjure you by the great, eternal, and almighty God, whom mountains and valleys fear throughout the inhabited world, because of whom the lion abandons its prey, and the mountains tremble, and the earth and the sea grow agitated, each one longing for the fear of the eternal, immortal, all-seeing, evil-hating Lord, who knows the good and bad that has happened on sea, rivers, mountains, and land. Aoth Abraoth, the God of Abraham, and Iao, the God of Jacob. Iao Aoth Abraoth, God of Israel, bring, yoke Orbanos, whom Urbana bore, to Domitiana, whom Candidus bore, loving, frenzied, tormented for the love and desire of Domitiana, whom Candidus bore. Yoke them in marriage and love, to live together for all the time of their life. Make him like a slave to her, willing to be subject, desiring no other woman or virgin, but only Domitiana, whom Candidus bore, to have as his wife for all the time of their life. Now, now, quickly, quickly!
EDCS-39100001.summary: This is a love-binding or attraction spell, likely from the Roman Imperial period, using a complex mix of Greek and Latin with divine names to compel Orbanos to return to Domitiana.

EDCS-39100002.translation: Alimbeou, coloumbeou, petallimbeou, legise, Adonai Sabaoth, Semesila. That the heavy ones of the Daourian horses, the Daourians, may not move their feet. Cast them down, and chain their feet.
EDCS-39100002.summary: This is a curse tablet, likely from the Roman Imperial period, aimed at hindering specific Daourian horses and their handlers in a race, using divine names and Greek.

EDCS-39100009.translation: I adjure you, whoever you are, death-daemon, eternally, by God and by the beings in Awdynasoi. Parak oainua, yagathea, simouebouarre, ekarophaisi, ewnythka, seuroai, echmasirouchta, e, athelchtasne, suek. Bind the horses of the rose-colored one and the white one, whose names I have deposited for you: Erythraios, Arboustos, Parathos, Parasitos, Pre, Valente, Amatore, Indomitō. Bind their soul, their race, their power, their charge, their speed. Take away their victory, hinder their feet, cut off their sinews, dislocate their joints, so that they may not be able, on the coming day, to enter the hippodrome, nor run, nor walk, nor win, nor exit the gates of the hippaphoroi, nor advance on the aria, nor the spatium, nor circle the turning posts, but let them fall with their own charioteers, Dionysios of the white one, and Superstianos. They command you, O oreobazagra, alabath, barbaros, maskellei. Bind the horses of the rose-colored one and the white one, whose names I have deposited for you: Lynkaion, R-, argare, aoud, Erythraios, Arboustos, Parathos, Parasitos, Ate, r, v, n, Valente, Korinthos, Temerarion, Indomitō. Bind their race, their feet, their victory, their charge, their soul, their speed, so that they may not be able, on the coming day, to enter the hippodrome, nor run, nor walk, nor win, nor circle the turning posts, but let them fall with their own charioteers, Dionysios and Superstianos. Bind their hands, take away their victory, their dismounting, and their sight, so that they may not be able to see their own opponents while driving, but rather let them fall with their own horses. Now, quickly!
EDCS-39100009.summary: This is a curse tablet, likely from the Roman Imperial period, intended to sabotage specific horses and their charioteers in a chariot race by binding their abilities and causing them to crash, referencing specific colored teams ('rose-colored' and 'white').

EDCS-39100011.translation: O demon, whoever you are, by these names I invoke you: Bōnara-ḵa, Abra-bapegoē, Pseu-ern, Ther-n, Bθερ, Therban, Kōnthōi, Euōeiōe, Rara, Ablaraē, Apaba-r, Ḵaer-m-noron, M-so, K-ballo, Dekar-babu, Sakhia-e. Come, that you may bind the horses of the Green team, whose names I entrust to you: Dareios, Āgilos, Pardos, Pougiōn, Dardanos, Eīnakhos, Pretiōsos, Prounikos, and his consort Venetus, Wittātos, Deireisōrēs, Wiktōr, Armēnios. Bind them, speed, victory, impulse, soul, swiftness. Cripple them, dislocate their joints, so that on the morrow they will not be able to race or walk or win in the hippodrome, nor pass through the gates of the hippoiaphioi, nor advance on the aria, nor the spatium, nor round the turning posts, but may they fall with their own charioteers, Prōtos of the Green team and Dionysios of the Venetus. For the demons command you: Uphris, Thenbene-b-nekhyrtōi, Oibesmerein, Iazana-bel, Iaō, Aukaē-m-sor, Mekha-m-risram, Phērtor-gōs, Euser-benleioi. Bind the horses of the Green team: Dareios, Āgilos, Pardos, Pougiōn, Dardanos, Eīnakhos, Pretiōsos, Prounikos, and his consort Venetus, Wittātos, Deireisōrēs, Wiktōr, Armēnios. Bind them, speed, victory, impulse, soul, swiftness. Cripple them, dislocate their joints, so that when they come to the hippodrome, harnessed, they will not be able to race or walk or win, nor pass through the gates of the hippoiaphioi, nor advance on the aria, nor the spatium, nor round the turning posts, but may they fall with their own charioteers, Prōtos of the Green team and Dionysios of the Venetus. Bind their hands, remove their victory, their start, and their sight, so that they cannot see their own opponents while driving, but rather snatch them from their own chariots and cast them to the ground, so that they fall with their own horses. Now! Now! Quickly! Quickly! Dionysios, Prōtos.
EDCS-39100011.summary: This is a magical Greek curse tablet, likely from the 2nd or 3rd century CE, intended to harm the horses and charioteers of a rival racing faction by invoking a powerful demon.

EDCS-39100012.translation: I exorcise you, whoever you are, dead-demon, the god who created earth and sky, Iona. I exorcise you, the god who has authority over the nether regions, Neicharoplex. I exorcise you, the god of spirits, A-B. I exorcise you, the god of Necessity, the great Arourobarzagran. I swear you by the god who is firstborn of the Earth, Ephōn-keisai-blā-bleis-pheib-al. I swear you by the god of winds and spirits, Lailam. I swear you by the god of punishments of every living thing, Rapokmēph. I swear you by the god, master of the celestial firmaments, Achramachameirei. I swear you by the chthonic god, who rules over every living thing, Sal-al-akhaw-brē. I swear you by the god, the conductor of the dead, the holy Hermes, the celestial, Aōn, krei-ton, earthly, aleon, bnin, the chthonic, Archphēsōn. I swear you by the god who is over the bestowal of the soul of every human, Iao. I swear you by the god who illuminates and darkens the world, Sēme-seilam. I swear you by the god, the origin of all human magic, Saiuphn, Sabaōth. I swear you by the god of Solomon, Suarmimō-uth. I swear you by the god who has the power in the second firmament, Marmaraōth. I swear you by the god of rebirth, Thōbarrabau. I swear you by the god of all the winepresses, Ieu. I swear you by the god of this day, Iaōabāōth. I swear you by the god who has authority over this hour, Iēso. I swear you by the god, master of the celestial firmaments, Iaō, Iboē-a. I swear you by the celestial god, Ithyaō. I swear you by the god who bestowed reason upon every human, Nege-m-psen-pueni-pē. I swear you by the god who formed every race of humans, Khōi-khare-amōn. I swear you by the god who bestowed sight upon every human, Ēkheta-rōpsi-eu. I swear you by the god who bestowed the movement of the limbs upon humans, Thesthenothril, Khe-aunxin. I swear you by the ancestral god, Phnūphobōēn. I swear you by the god who granted you sleep and released you from the bonds of life, Neth-maō. I swear you by the god who rules every myth, Nākhar. I swear you by the god who is master of sleep, Sthombloēn. I swear you by the aerial, pelagic, subterranean, celestial god, the beginning of the seas, conjoined, the only begotten, who appeared from him, who has power over fire, water, earth, and air, Ōi-aōeēnafet-i. I further exorcise you by the earthly names of Hekate, Trimorphos, the scourger, the enslaved, the torchbearer, Chrysan-dalai-mo-potikhthōn-ian, the ippeitroakt-i, phere-skhegal, Nebūtos-uant. I will tell you the true name by which Tartarus, earth, abyss, and sky tremble: Phorba-bor-phorba-bor, O-ror-basu-netei-rō, Molt-iēaiō, Phylakē, Napu-pheraiō, Anankē, Maskelli, Maskellō, Phnūken-tabāōth, Oreobarzar-gra, Ēsthan-khukhēn-khu-kheōkh. That you may serve me in the circus on the 17th of November and bind every limb, every sinew, the shoulders, the wrists, the elbows of the charioteers of the rousseau, Olympios and Olympiānus, and Skortios and Iuuenkos. Torment their minds, their intellects, their senses, so that they do not know what they are doing. Blind their eyes, so that they cannot see, neither they nor the horses they will drive: Aigyptos, Kallidromos, and if anyone else is yoked with them, Valentinus and Lampad, and Mauros son of Lampas, and Chrysespis son of Iūban, and Indos, Palmatos, and Superbus, and Eion, Boubalos, Kēnsōrapou, Erina, and if any other horse is going to be driven by them, and if any other horse is to be yoked with these, may they be preempted and not come to victory.
EDCS-39100012.summary: This is a complex and lengthy Greek magical curse text, likely from Egypt, invoking numerous deities and powerful names to curse horses and charioteers in a chariot race, probably in the late Roman period.
